title: 孟子
note: Chinese text only. English translations are generated by the translator-classical agent at pipeline runtime.

passages.text: 孟子見梁惠王。王曰：「叟不遠千里而來，亦將有以利吾國乎？」孟子對曰：「王何必曰利？亦有仁義而已矣。王曰『何以利吾國』？大夫曰『何以利吾家』？士庶人曰『何以利吾身』？上下交征利而國危矣。萬乘之國弒其君者，必千乘之家；千乘之國弒其君者，必百乘之家。萬取千焉，千取百焉，不為不多矣。苟為後義而先利，不奪不饜。未有仁而遺其親者也，未有義而後其君者也。王亦曰仁義而已矣，何必曰利？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius visited King Hui of Liang. The king said, 'Sir, you have not considered a thousand li too far to come — surely you have something that will profit my state?' Mencius replied, 'Why must Your Majesty speak of profit? There is only benevolence and righteousness, nothing more. If the king says, "How can I profit my state?" the great officers say, "How can I profit my house?" and the common scholars and people say, "How can I profit myself?" — then those above and below will compete with one another for profit, and the state will be endangered. In a state of ten thousand chariots, the one who murders its ruler will surely be the head of a house with a thousand chariots; in a state of a thousand chariots, the one who murders its ruler will surely be the head of a house with a hundred chariots. To take a thousand from ten thousand, or a hundred from a thousand — that is no small share. But if righteousness is put last and profit is put first, they will not be satisfied without seizing everything. There has never been a benevolent person who abandoned his parents, nor a righteous person who neglected his ruler. Let Your Majesty speak only of benevolence and righteousness — why must you speak of profit?'

passages.text: 孟子見梁惠王，王立於沼上，顧鴻鴈麋鹿，曰：「賢者亦樂此乎？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius visited King Hui of Liang. The king was standing by a pond, gazing at the geese, wild ducks, and deer, and said, 'Do the worthy also take pleasure in such things?'

passages.text: 孟子對曰：「賢者而後樂此，不賢者雖有此，不樂也。《詩》云：『經始靈臺，經之營之，庶民攻之，不日成之。經始勿亟，庶民子來。王在靈囿，麀鹿攸伏，麀鹿濯濯，白鳥鶴鶴。王在靈沼，於牣魚躍。』文王以民力為臺為沼。而民歡樂之，謂其臺曰靈臺，謂其沼曰靈沼，樂其有麋鹿魚鼈。古之人與民偕樂，故能樂也。《湯誓》曰：『時日害喪？予及女偕亡。』民欲與之偕亡，雖有臺池鳥獸，豈能獨樂哉？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius replied, 'Only the worthy can truly take pleasure in such things. Those who are not worthy, even if they possess them, cannot find true pleasure. The Book of Odes says: "He began the Spirit Tower, planning and measuring it; the common people worked on it and completed it in no time. He began it without haste, yet the people came as if they were his children. The king was in the Spirit Park, where the does lay at rest; the does were sleek and glossy, the white birds glistened. The king was at the Spirit Pond, where the fish leapt in abundance." King Wen used the labor of the people to build his tower and pond, yet the people delighted in it, calling his tower the Spirit Tower and his pond the Spirit Pond, rejoicing that he had deer, fish, and turtles. The ancients shared their pleasures with the people, and therefore could truly enjoy them. The Declaration of Tang says: "O sun, when will you perish? I am willing to perish together with you!" When the people wished to perish together with their ruler, even though he had towers, ponds, birds, and beasts, how could he enjoy them alone?'

passages.text: 梁惠王曰：「寡人之於國也，盡心焉耳矣。河內凶，則移其民於河東，移其粟於河內。河東凶亦然。察鄰國之政，無如寡人之用心者。鄰國之民不加少，寡人之民不加多，何也？」孟子對曰：「王好戰，請以戰喻。填然鼓之，兵刃既接，棄甲曳兵而走。或百步而後止，或五十步而後止。以五十步笑百步，則何如？」曰：「不可，直不百步耳，是亦走也。」
passages.translation_en: King Hui of Liang said, 'I devote my whole heart to governing my state. When there is famine in Henei, I move the people to Hedong and transfer grain to Henei. When there is famine in Hedong, I do the same. When I examine the policies of neighboring states, none governs as attentively as I do. Yet the people of neighboring states do not decrease, and my people do not increase — why is this?' Mencius replied, 'Your Majesty is fond of war, so let me use a war analogy. When the drums thunder and the blades clash, some soldiers throw down their armor and flee. Some stop after a hundred paces, some after fifty paces. What would you think if those who ran fifty paces laughed at those who ran a hundred?' The king said, 'That would not be right. They merely did not run a hundred paces — but they ran all the same.'

passages.text: 曰：「王如知此，則無望民之多於鄰國也。不違農時，穀不可勝食也；數罟不入洿池，魚鼈不可勝食也；斧斤以時入山林，材木不可勝用也。穀與魚鼈不可勝食，材木不可勝用，是使民養生喪死無憾也。養生喪死無憾，王道之始也。五畝之宅，樹之以桑，五十者可以衣帛矣；雞豚狗彘之畜，無失其時，七十者可以食肉矣；百畝之田，勿奪其時，數口之家可以無飢矣；謹庠序之教，申之以孝悌之義，頒白者不負戴於道路矣。七十者衣帛食肉，黎民不飢不寒，然而不王者，未之有也。
passages.translation_en: Mencius said, 'If Your Majesty understands this, then do not expect your people to be more numerous than those of neighboring states. If farming is not disrupted in its seasons, there will be more grain than can be eaten. If fine-meshed nets are not cast into the ponds, there will be more fish and turtles than can be consumed. If axes and hatchets enter the mountain forests only in the proper season, there will be more timber than can be used. When grain, fish, and turtles cannot all be consumed, and timber cannot all be used, this allows the people to nourish the living and mourn the dead without regret. Nourishing the living and mourning the dead without regret — this is the beginning of the Kingly Way. Plant mulberry trees around homesteads of five mu, and those over fifty can wear silk. Raise chickens, pigs, and dogs without missing their breeding seasons, and those over seventy can eat meat. Do not take away the labor time from farms of a hundred mu, and families of several mouths need not go hungry. Attend carefully to the education in the village schools, and instruct the people in the duties of filial piety and brotherly respect, and those with graying hair will not be seen carrying heavy loads on the roads. When those over seventy wear silk and eat meat, and the common people are neither hungry nor cold — no ruler who achieves this has ever failed to become a true king.'

passages.text: 狗彘食人食而不知檢，塗有餓莩而不知發；人死，則曰：『非我也，歲也。』是何異於刺人而殺之，曰：『非我也，兵也。』王無罪歲，斯天下之民至焉。」梁惠王曰：「寡人願安承教。」孟子對曰：「殺人以梃與刃，有以異乎？」曰：「無以異也。」「以刃與政，有以異乎？」曰：「無以異也。」
passages.translation_en: 'When pigs and dogs eat the food of humans and no one thinks to restrain it, when people lie starving on the roads and no one thinks to open the granaries — when people die, to say "It is not my fault, it is the harvest" — how is this different from stabbing a man and killing him, then saying "It is not me, it is the weapon"? If Your Majesty would stop blaming the harvests, then the people of all the world would come to you.' King Hui of Liang said, 'I would be glad to receive your instruction.' Mencius replied, 'Is there any difference between killing a person with a club and killing him with a blade?' The king said, 'There is no difference.' 'Is there any difference between killing with a blade and killing with misgovernment?' The king said, 'There is no difference.'

passages.text: 曰：「庖有肥肉，廐有肥馬，民有飢色，野有餓莩，此率獸而食人也。獸相食，且人惡之。為民父母，行政不免於率獸而食人。惡在其為民父母也？仲尼曰：『始作俑者，其無後乎！』為其象人而用之也。如之何其使斯民飢而死也？」梁惠王曰：「晉國，天下莫強焉，叟之所知也。及寡人之身，東敗於齊，長子死焉；西喪地於秦七百里；南辱於楚。寡人恥之，願比死者一洒之，如之何則可？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said, 'In your kitchen there is fat meat; in your stables there are sleek horses. Yet the people have the look of hunger, and in the countryside the starved lie dead. This is to lead beasts to devour men. When beasts devour one another, people find it hateful. If one who serves as parent to the people conducts government in a way no different from leading beasts to devour men, then where is his claim to be the parent of the people? Confucius said, "Was not the man who first made burial figurines left without posterity!" — because the figurines resembled humans and were used in place of them. How then can one allow his people to starve to death?' King Hui of Liang said, 'The state of Wei was once the strongest in the world, as you well know, sir. But in my time, we suffered defeat to Qi in the east, and my eldest son perished there; we lost seven hundred li of territory to Qin in the west; and we were humiliated by Chu in the south. I am ashamed of this and wish to avenge these wrongs on behalf of those who died. What can I do?'

passages.text: 孟子對曰：「地方百里而可以王。王如施仁政於民，省刑罰，薄稅斂，深耕易耨。壯者以暇日修其孝悌忠信，入以事其父兄，出以事其長上，可使制梃以撻秦楚之堅甲利兵矣。彼奪其民時，使不得耕耨以養其父母，父母凍餓，兄弟妻子離散。彼陷溺其民，王往而征之，夫誰與王敵？故曰：『仁者無敵。』王請勿疑！」孟子見梁襄王。出，語人曰：「望之不似人君，就之而不見所畏焉。卒然問曰：『天下惡乎定？』吾對曰：『定于一。』
passages.translation_en: Mencius replied, 'A territory of even a hundred li square is sufficient to become a true king. If Your Majesty practices benevolent government toward the people — reducing punishments, lightening taxes and levies, encouraging deep plowing and thorough weeding — then the able-bodied can use their spare days to cultivate filial piety, brotherly respect, loyalty, and faithfulness, serving their fathers and elder brothers at home and their elders and superiors abroad. They could then be made to take up clubs and defeat the strong armor and sharp weapons of Qin and Chu. Those other states steal their people's time, preventing them from plowing and weeding to feed their parents. Parents freeze and starve; brothers, wives, and children are scattered and separated. Those rulers drown and trap their own people — if Your Majesty were to march against them, who would stand against you? Therefore it is said: "The benevolent have no enemies." I beg Your Majesty not to doubt this!' Mencius met King Xiang of Liang. After leaving, he said to someone, 'When I looked at him from afar, he did not look like a ruler of men; when I drew close, I saw nothing commanding about him. Abruptly he asked, "How can the world be settled?" I replied, "It will be settled through unity."'

passages.text: 『孰能一之？』對曰：『不嗜殺人者能一之。』『孰能與之？』對曰：『天下莫不與也。王知夫苗乎？七八月之間旱，則苗槁矣。天油然作雲，沛然下雨，則苗浡然興之矣。其如是，孰能禦之？今夫天下之人牧，未有不嗜殺人者也，如有不嗜殺人者，則天下之民皆引領而望之矣。誠如是也，民歸之，由水之就下，沛然誰能禦之？』」齊宣王問曰：「齊桓、晉文之事可得聞乎？」
passages.translation_en: '"Who can unify it?" I replied, "One who does not delight in killing can unify it." "Who would give their allegiance to such a person?" I replied, "Everyone in the world would give their allegiance. Does Your Majesty know about the young rice shoots? If there is a drought in the seventh or eighth month, the shoots wither. But when the sky masses thick clouds and sends down a torrent of rain, the shoots spring up vigorously. When this happens, who can stop it? Among the shepherds of men in the world today, there is not one who does not delight in killing. If there were one who did not delight in killing, all the people in the world would crane their necks looking toward him. If this were truly so, the people would flow to him like water flowing downward — in a torrent that no one could hold back."' King Xuan of Qi asked, 'May I hear about the affairs of Duke Huan of Qi and Duke Wen of Jin?'

passages.text: 孟子對曰：「仲尼之徒無道桓、文之事者，是以後世無傳焉。臣未之聞也。無以，則王乎？」曰：「德何如，則可以王矣？」曰：「保民而王，莫之能禦也。」曰：「若寡人者，可以保民乎哉？」曰：「可。」曰：「何由知吾可也？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius replied, 'None of the followers of Confucius spoke of the affairs of Duke Huan and Duke Wen, and so nothing was passed down to later generations. Your servant has heard nothing of them. If you will not let the matter rest, then shall we speak of true kingship?' The king asked, 'What must one's virtue be like to practice true kingship?' Mencius said, 'One who protects the people can become a true king, and no one can stop him.' The king asked, 'Could someone like me truly protect the people?' Mencius said, 'You could.' The king asked, 'How do you know that I could?'

passages.text: 曰：「臣聞之胡齕曰，王坐於堂上，有牽牛而過堂下者，王見之，曰：『牛何之？』對曰：『將以釁鐘。』王曰：『舍之！吾不忍其觳觫，若無罪而就死地。』對曰：『然則廢釁鐘與？』曰：『何可廢也？以羊易之！』不識有諸？」曰：「有之。」曰：「是心足以王矣。百姓皆以王為愛也，臣固知王之不忍也。」王曰：「然。誠有百姓者。齊國雖褊小，吾何愛一牛？即不忍其觳觫，若無罪而就死地，故以羊易之也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said, 'Your servant heard the following from Hu He: Your Majesty was sitting in the upper hall when someone led an ox past below. You saw it and asked, "Where is the ox going?" The man replied, "We are going to consecrate a bell with its blood." You said, "Let it go! I cannot bear its terrified trembling — it is like an innocent man going to his execution." The man asked, "Then shall we abandon the bell consecration?" You said, "How can we abandon it? Use a sheep instead!" Did this really happen?' The king said, 'It did.' Mencius said, 'This heart is sufficient to become a true king. The common people all thought Your Majesty was being stingy, but your servant knew that you simply could not bear the animal's suffering.' The king said, 'That is right. There really were such people who thought so. But though Qi is a small and narrow state, how could I begrudge a single ox? It was simply that I could not bear its terrified trembling, like an innocent creature going to its death — that is why I exchanged it for a sheep.'

passages.text: 曰：「王無異於百姓之以王為愛也。以小易大，彼惡知之？王若隱其無罪而就死地，則牛羊何擇焉？」王笑曰：「是誠何心哉？我非愛其財。而易之以羊也，宜乎百姓之謂我愛也。」曰：「無傷也，是乃仁術也，見牛未見羊也。君子之於禽獸也，見其生，不忍見其死；聞其聲，不忍食其肉。是以君子遠庖廚也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said, 'Your Majesty should not be surprised that the people thought you stingy. You replaced the large with the small — how could they understand? If Your Majesty was pained that an innocent animal was going to its death, then what was there to choose between the ox and the sheep?' The king laughed and said, 'What was my true motive, I wonder? I was not grudging the expense when I exchanged it for a sheep — but I suppose it was natural for the people to call me stingy.' Mencius said, 'There is no harm in it. This was in fact the method of benevolence: you had seen the ox but had not seen the sheep. The gentleman, in his relation to animals — having seen them alive, he cannot bear to see them die; having heard their cries, he cannot bear to eat their flesh. That is why the gentleman keeps his distance from the kitchen.'

passages.text: 王說曰：「《詩》云：『他人有心，予忖度之。』夫子之謂也。夫我乃行之，反而求之，不得吾心。夫子言之，於我心有戚戚焉。此心之所以合於王者，何也？」曰：「有復於王者曰：『吾力足以舉百鈞』，而不足以舉一羽；『明足以察秋毫之末』，而不見輿薪，則王許之乎？」曰：「否。」
passages.translation_en: The king was pleased and said, 'The Ode says: "What other men have in their hearts, I measure by reflection." This describes you, Master. For I was the one who acted, yet when I turned inward to examine myself, I could not grasp my own motive. When you, Master, spoke of it, my heart stirred with recognition. How is it that this heart of mine accords with true kingship?' Mencius said, 'Suppose someone reported to Your Majesty: "My strength is sufficient to lift three thousand catties, but not sufficient to lift a single feather; my eyesight is sharp enough to discern the tip of an autumn hair, but I cannot see a cartload of firewood." Would Your Majesty accept this?' The king said, 'No.'

passages.text: 「今恩足以及禽獸，而功不至於百姓者，獨何與？然則一羽之不舉，為不用力焉；輿薪之不見，為不用明焉，百姓之不見保，為不用恩焉。故王之不王，不為也，非不能也。」曰：「不為者與不能者之形何以異？」
passages.translation_en: 'Now, your kindness is sufficient to reach animals, yet its benefits do not reach the common people — why is this the sole exception? A feather not lifted — it is because one does not use one's strength. A cartload of firewood not seen — it is because one does not use one's sight. The people not cared for — it is because one does not use one's kindness. Therefore, Your Majesty's failure to be a true king is because you choose not to act, not because you cannot.' The king asked, 'How does the form of choosing not to act differ from that of being unable?'

passages.text: 曰：「挾太山以超北海，語人曰『我不能』，是誠不能也。為長者折枝，語人曰『我不能』，是不為也，非不能也。故王之不王，非挾太山以超北海之類也；王之不王，是折枝之類也。老吾老，以及人之老；幼吾幼，以及人之幼。天下可運於掌。《詩》云：『刑于寡妻，至于兄弟，以御于家邦。』言舉斯心加諸彼而已。故推恩足以保四海，不推恩無以保妻子。古之人所以大過人者無他焉，善推其所為而已矣。今恩足以及禽獸，而功不至於百姓者，獨何與？權，然後知輕重；度，然後知長短。物皆然，心為甚。王請度之！抑王興甲兵，危士臣，構怨於諸侯，然後快於心與？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said, 'If someone says, "I cannot do it," when asked to tuck Mount Tai under his arm and leap over the North Sea — that is truly being unable. If someone says, "I cannot do it," when asked to bend a branch for an elder — that is choosing not to act, not being unable. Therefore, Your Majesty's failure to be a true king is not of the class of tucking Mount Tai under your arm and leaping over the North Sea; it is of the class of bending a branch. Treat your own elders as elders, and extend this to the elders of others; treat your own young ones as young ones, and extend this to the young of others — then the world can be turned in the palm of your hand. The Ode says: "He set an example for his wife, extended it to his brothers, and so governed the clan and the state." This simply means taking this heart and applying it to others. Therefore, extending kindness is sufficient to protect all within the four seas; not extending kindness, one cannot even protect one's own wife and children. The reason the ancients so greatly surpassed others was nothing else — they were simply good at extending what they did. Now, your kindness is sufficient to reach animals, yet its benefits do not reach the common people — why is this the sole exception? Weigh, and then you know light from heavy; measure, and then you know long from short. It is so with all things, but especially so with the heart. I beg Your Majesty to measure it! Or does Your Majesty find satisfaction in raising arms, endangering your officers and ministers, and incurring the enmity of the other lords?'

passages.text: 王曰：「否。吾何快於是？將以求吾所大欲也。」曰：「王之所大欲可得聞與？」王笑而不言。曰：「為肥甘不足於口與？輕煖不足於體與？抑為采色不足視於目與？聲音不足聽於耳與？便嬖不足使令於前與？王之諸臣皆足以供之，而王豈為是哉？」曰：「否。吾不為是也。」曰：「然則王之所大欲可知已。欲辟土地，朝秦楚，莅中國而撫四夷也。以若所為求若所欲，猶緣木而求魚也。」王曰：「若是其甚與？」
passages.translation_en: The king said, 'No. Why would I find satisfaction in that? I do it to pursue what I most desire.' Mencius asked, 'May I hear what it is that Your Majesty most desires?' The king smiled and did not answer. Mencius said, 'Is it because rich foods are not enough for your mouth? Lightweight furs are not warm enough for your body? Or is it because brilliant colors are not enough for your eyes? Sweet music is not enough for your ears? Favored attendants are not enough to serve you? Your Majesty's ministers can all supply these — surely it is not for these things?' The king said, 'No, it is not for these.' Mencius said, 'Then what Your Majesty most desires can be known. You wish to expand your territory, to make Qin and Chu pay court to you, to rule the Central States and bring the surrounding peoples under your care. But to pursue what you desire by the means you are using — that is like climbing a tree to catch a fish.' The king said, 'Is it really as bad as that?'

passages.text: 曰：「殆有甚焉。緣木求魚，雖不得魚，無後災。以若所為，求若所欲，盡心力而為之，後必有災。」曰：「可得聞與？」曰：「鄒人與楚人戰，則王以為孰勝？」曰：「楚人勝。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said, 'It is probably even worse. If you climb a tree to seek fish, though you will not catch any fish, there will be no disaster afterward. But if you pursue what you desire by the means you are using, exerting all your heart and strength, there will surely be disaster in the end.' The king said, 'May I hear about this?' Mencius said, 'If the people of Zou were to fight the people of Chu, who does Your Majesty think would win?' The king said, 'The people of Chu would win.'

passages.text: 曰：「然則小固不可以敵大，寡固不可以敵眾，弱固不可以敵彊。海內之地方千里者九，齊集有其一。以一服八，何以異於鄒敵楚哉？蓋亦反其本矣。今王發政施仁，使天下仕者皆欲立於王之朝，耕者皆欲耕於王之野，商賈皆欲藏於王之市，行旅皆欲出於王之塗，天下之欲疾其君者皆欲赴愬於王。其若是，孰能禦之？」王曰：「吾惛，不能進於是矣。願夫子輔吾志，明以教我。我雖不敏，請嘗試之。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said, 'So then, the small certainly cannot match the large, the few cannot match the many, and the weak cannot match the strong. Within the seas, the territories of a thousand li square number nine, and Qi possesses but one of them. To use one to subdue eight — how is this different from Zou fighting Chu? You must go back to the root of the matter. If now Your Majesty were to issue benevolent government, causing all the officials in the world to wish to serve in your court, all the farmers to wish to plow in your fields, all the merchants to wish to store their goods in your markets, all the travelers to wish to journey on your roads, and all those who are aggrieved by their own rulers to wish to bring their complaints to you — if it were truly so, who could withstand you?' The king said, 'I am dull and cannot advance to this. I hope you, Master, will support my resolve and instruct me clearly. Though I am not clever, let me try.'

passages.text: 曰：「無恆產而有恆心者，惟士為能。若民，則無恆產，因無恆心。苟無恆心，放辟，邪侈，無不為已。及陷於罪，然後從而刑之，是罔民也。焉有仁人在位，罔民而可為也？是故明君制民之產，必使仰足以事父母，俯足以畜妻子，樂歲終身飽，凶年免於死亡。然後驅而之善，故民之從之也輕。今也制民之產，仰不足以事父母，俯不足以畜妻子，樂歲終身苦，凶年不免於死亡。此惟救死而恐不贍，奚暇治禮義哉？王欲行之，則盍反其本矣。五畝之宅，樹之以桑，五十者可以衣帛矣；雞豚狗彘之畜，無失其時，七十者可以食肉矣；百畝之田，勿奪其時，八口之家可以無飢矣；謹庠序之教，申之以孝悌之義，頒白者不負戴於道路矣。老者衣帛食肉，黎民不飢不寒，然而不王者，未之有也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said, 'Those who have a constant livelihood without a constant heart — only the educated are capable of this. As for the common people, without a constant livelihood, they will lack a constant heart. And if they lack a constant heart, there is nothing — dissipation, deviation, depravity, excess — they will not do. When they have thus fallen into crime and you then punish them, this is entrapping the people. How can there be a benevolent person in power who entraps the people? Therefore an enlightened ruler, in regulating the people's livelihood, must ensure that above they have enough to serve their parents, and below they have enough to support their wives and children; that in good years they are always well-fed, and in bad years they escape death. Only then does he urge them toward goodness, and so the people follow him readily. But now, the people's livelihood is regulated so that above they do not have enough to serve their parents, and below they do not have enough to support their wives and children; in good years they suffer all their lives, and in bad years they cannot escape death. Under these conditions, they are simply trying to survive and fear they cannot manage — what leisure have they for cultivating rites and righteousness? If Your Majesty wishes to carry this out, then why not return to the root? Plant mulberry trees around homesteads of five mu, and those over fifty can wear silk. Raise chickens, pigs, and dogs without missing their breeding seasons, and those over seventy can eat meat. Do not take away the labor time from farms of a hundred mu, and families of eight mouths need not go hungry. Attend carefully to the education in the village schools, and instruct the people in the duties of filial piety and brotherly respect, and those with graying hair will not be seen carrying heavy loads on the roads. When the aged wear silk and eat meat, and the common people are neither hungry nor cold — no ruler who achieves this has ever failed to become a true king.'

passages.text: 莊暴見孟子，曰：「暴見於王，王語暴以好樂，暴未有以對也。」曰：「好樂何如？」孟子曰：「王之好樂甚，則齊國其庶幾乎！」他日，見於王曰：「王嘗語莊子以好樂，有諸？」王變乎色，曰：「寡人非能好先王之樂也，直好世俗之樂耳。」曰：「王之好樂甚，則齊其庶幾乎！今之樂猶古之樂也。」曰：「可得聞與？」曰：「獨樂樂，與人樂樂，孰樂？」曰：「不若與人。」曰：「與少樂樂，與眾樂樂，孰樂？」曰：「不若與眾。」
passages.translation_en: Zhuang Bao went to see Mencius and said, "I had an audience with the king, and the king told me of his love for music. I had no reply to offer." He then asked, "What about loving music?" Mencius said, "If the king's love of music were great enough, then the state of Qi would be close to good governance!" On another day, Mencius had an audience with the king and said, "Your Majesty once told Zhuang Bao of your love for music—is this true?" The king's expression changed, and he said, "I am not able to love the music of the ancient kings. I merely love popular music." Mencius said, "If Your Majesty's love of music were great enough, then Qi would be close to good governance! The music of today is just like the music of antiquity." The king said, "May I hear more about this?" Mencius said, "Which is more enjoyable—to enjoy music alone, or to enjoy it with others?" The king said, "It is better to enjoy it with others." Mencius said, "Which is more enjoyable—to enjoy music with a few, or to enjoy it with many?" The king said, "It is better to enjoy it with many."

passages.text: 「臣請為王言樂：今王鼓樂於此，百姓聞王鐘鼓之聲，管籥之音，舉疾首蹙頞而相告曰：『吾王之好鼓樂，夫何使我至於此極也？父子不相見，兄弟妻子離散。』今王田獵於此，百姓聞王車馬之音，見羽旄之美，舉疾首蹙頞而相告曰：『吾王之好田獵，夫何使我至於此極也？父子不相見，兄弟妻子離散。』此無他，不與民同樂也。」
passages.translation_en: "Allow me to speak to Your Majesty about music. Suppose Your Majesty were playing music here, and the people, hearing the sound of your bells and drums, your flutes and pipes, all clutched their aching heads and furrowed their brows, saying to one another, 'Our king's love of music—how has it brought us to such a miserable state? Fathers and sons cannot see each other; brothers, wives, and children are scattered and separated.' Suppose Your Majesty were hunting here, and the people, hearing the sound of your horses and carriages, seeing the splendor of your feathered banners, all clutched their aching heads and furrowed their brows, saying to one another, 'Our king's love of hunting—how has it brought us to such a miserable state? Fathers and sons cannot see each other; brothers, wives, and children are scattered and separated.' The reason for this is nothing other than that you do not share your pleasures with the people."

passages.text: 「今王鼓樂於此，百姓聞王鐘鼓之聲，管籥之音，舉欣欣然有喜色而相告曰：『吾王庶幾無疾病與？何以能鼓樂也？』今王田獵於此，百姓聞王車馬之音，見羽旄之美，舉欣欣然有喜色而相告曰『吾王庶幾無疾病與？何以能田獵也？』此無他，與民同樂也。今王與百姓同樂，則王矣。」齊宣王問曰：「文王之囿方七十里，有諸？」孟子對曰：「於傳有之。」曰：「若是其大乎？」曰：「民猶以為小也。」
passages.translation_en: "Now suppose Your Majesty were playing music here, and the people, hearing the sound of your bells and drums, your flutes and pipes, all looked cheerful and happy, saying to one another, 'Our king must be in good health! Otherwise, how could he play music?' Suppose Your Majesty were hunting here, and the people, hearing the sound of your horses and carriages, seeing the splendor of your feathered banners, all looked cheerful and happy, saying to one another, 'Our king must be in good health! Otherwise, how could he go hunting?' The reason for this is nothing other than that you share your pleasures with the people. If Your Majesty shares his pleasures with the people, you will be a true king." King Xuan of Qi asked, "Is it true that King Wen's park was seventy li square?" Mencius replied, "So it says in the records." The king said, "Was it really that large?" Mencius said, "The people still considered it too small."

passages.text: 曰：「寡人之囿方四十里，民猶以為大，何也？」曰：「文王之囿方七十里，芻蕘者往焉，雉兔者往焉，與民同之。民以為小，不亦宜乎？臣始至於境，問國之大禁，然後敢入。臣聞郊關之內有囿方四十里，殺其麋鹿者如殺人之罪。則是方四十里，為阱於國中。民以為大，不亦宜乎？」齊宣王問曰：「交鄰國有道乎？」
passages.translation_en: The king said, "My park is only forty li square, yet the people consider it too large. Why is that?" Mencius said, "King Wen's park was seventy li square, but those who gathered grass and firewood could go there, and those who hunted pheasants and hares could go there. He shared it with the people. Is it not fitting that the people considered it small? When I first arrived at your border, I asked about the major prohibitions of the state before daring to enter. I heard that within the suburban gates there is a park of forty li square, and that anyone who kills a deer within it is punished as if he had committed murder. This forty-li park is like a trap set in the middle of the state. Is it not fitting that the people consider it too large?" King Xuan of Qi asked, "Is there a proper way to conduct relations with neighboring states?"

passages.text: 孟子對曰：「有。惟仁者為能以大事小，是故湯事葛，文王事昆夷；惟智者為能以小事大，故大王事獯鬻，句踐事吳。以大事小者，樂天者也；以小事大者，畏天者也。樂天者保天下，畏天者保其國。《詩》云：『畏天之威，于時保之。』」王曰：「大哉言矣！寡人有疾，寡人好勇。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius replied, "There is. Only a benevolent ruler can serve a smaller state while leading a larger one. That is why Tang served the state of Ge, and King Wen served the Kunyi tribes. Only a wise ruler can serve a larger state while leading a smaller one. That is why King Tai served the Xunyu, and Goujian served the state of Wu. He who serves a smaller state while leading a larger one delights in Heaven. He who serves a larger state while leading a smaller one stands in awe of Heaven. He who delights in Heaven protects the whole world. He who stands in awe of Heaven protects his own state. The Odes say, 'Standing in awe of Heaven's majesty, thereby he preserved it.'" The king said, "What great words! But I have a weakness—I love courage."

passages.text: 對曰：「王請無好小勇。夫撫劍疾視曰，『彼惡敢當我哉』！此匹夫之勇，敵一人者也。王請大之！《詩》云：『王赫斯怒，爰整其旅，以遏徂莒，以篤周祜，以對于天下。』此文王之勇也。文王一怒而安天下之民。《書》曰：『天降下民，作之君，作之師。惟曰其助上帝，寵之四方。有罪無罪，惟我在，天下曷敢有越厥志？』一人衡行於天下，武王恥之。此武王之勇也。而武王亦一怒而安天下之民。今王亦一怒而安天下之民，民惟恐王之不好勇也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius replied, "I beg Your Majesty not to love petty courage. To grip one's sword, glare fiercely, and say, 'How dare he stand against me!'—this is the courage of a common man, enough to face a single opponent. I beg Your Majesty to enlarge it! The Odes say, 'The king blazed with anger, and marshaled his forces, to halt the advance on Ju, to strengthen the fortunes of Zhou, to answer the expectations of the world.' This was the courage of King Wen. King Wen, in a single burst of anger, brought peace to the people of the world. The Documents say, 'Heaven sent down the people below and made for them rulers and teachers, saying: Help God to cherish them in every quarter. Whether guilty or innocent, that is my concern—who in the world dares exceed his proper role?' When one man ran rampant through the world, King Wu was ashamed of it. This was the courage of King Wu. And King Wu also, in a single burst of anger, brought peace to the people of the world. If Your Majesty likewise, in a single burst of anger, could bring peace to the people of the world, the people would only fear that Your Majesty does not love courage enough."

passages.text: 齊宣王見孟子於雪宮。王曰：「賢者亦有此樂乎？」孟子對曰：「有。人不得，則非其上矣。不得而非其上者，非也；為民上而不與民同樂者，亦非也。樂民之樂者，民亦樂其樂；憂民之憂者，民亦憂其憂。樂以天下，憂以天下，然而不王者，未之有也。
passages.translation_en: King Xuan of Qi received Mencius at the Snow Palace. The king said, "Do the worthy also enjoy such pleasures?" Mencius replied, "They do. When people cannot enjoy such things, they blame their superiors. To blame one's superiors for not being able to enjoy such things is wrong. But for a ruler to fail to share his pleasures with the people is also wrong. A ruler who takes joy in the people's joy—the people will also take joy in his joy. A ruler who grieves over the people's grief—the people will also grieve over his grief. One who takes joy with the whole world, and grieves with the whole world—such a person has never failed to become a true king."

passages.text: 「昔者齊景公問於晏子曰：『吾欲觀於轉附、朝儛，遵海而南，放于琅邪。吾何脩而可以比於先王觀也？』晏子對曰：『善哉問也！天子適諸侯曰巡狩，巡狩者巡所守也；諸侯朝於天子曰述職，述職者述所職也。無非事者。春省耕而補不足，秋省斂而助不給。夏諺曰：「吾王不遊，吾何以休？吾王不豫，吾何以助？一遊一豫，為諸侯度。」今也不然：師行而糧食，飢者弗食，勞者弗息。睊睊胥讒，民乃作慝。方命虐民，飲食若流。流連荒亡，為諸侯憂。從流下而忘反謂之流，從流上而忘反謂之連，從獸無厭謂之荒，樂酒無厭謂之亡。先王無流連之樂，荒亡之行。惟君所行也。』景公說，大戒於國，出舍於郊。於是始興發補不足。召大師曰：『為我作君臣相說之樂！』蓋徵招角招是也。其詩曰：『畜君何尤？』畜君者，好君也。」
passages.translation_en: "In ancient times, Duke Jing of Qi asked Yanzi, 'I wish to visit Mount Zhuanfu and Mount Chaowu, then follow the coast southward to Langya. How should I conduct myself so as to compare with the tours of the ancient kings?' Yanzi replied, 'An excellent question! When the Son of Heaven visits the feudal lords, it is called an inspection tour—he inspects what they are guarding. When the feudal lords go to the Son of Heaven, it is called a report on duties—they report on their assigned duties. None of these travels is without purpose. In spring, they inspect the plowing and supply what is lacking; in autumn, they inspect the harvest and assist those in need. The saying of the Xia dynasty goes: If our king does not tour, how shall we have rest? If our king does not travel, how shall we have help? Each tour and each journey set the standard for the feudal lords. But now it is not so: armies march and provisions are consumed, the hungry are not fed, the weary are not rested. People eye each other resentfully and slander grows, and the people turn to wickedness. Commands are flouted, the people are oppressed, and food and drink flow like water. Drifting, indulging, going wild, getting lost—these become a worry for the feudal lords. Going downstream and forgetting to return is called drifting. Going upstream and forgetting to return is called indulging. Hunting without limit is called going wild. Drinking without limit is called getting lost. The ancient kings had no pleasure in drifting or indulging, and no practice of going wild or getting lost. It is for Your Lordship to decide which path to take.' Duke Jing was pleased. He issued a great proclamation throughout the state, then went out and lodged in the suburbs. He then began to open the granaries to relieve the needy. He summoned the Grand Music Master and said, 'Compose for me music of harmony between ruler and minister!' This was presumably the Zhizhao and Jiaozhao. The lyrics said, 'What fault is it to restrain the ruler?' To restrain the ruler means to love the ruler."

passages.text: 齊宣王問曰：「人皆謂我毀明堂。毀諸？已乎？」孟子對曰：「夫明堂者，王者之堂也。王欲行王政，則勿毀之矣。」王曰：「王政可得聞與？」對曰：「昔者文王之治岐也，耕者九一，仕者世祿，關市譏而不征，澤梁無禁，罪人不孥。老而無妻曰鰥。老而無夫曰寡。老而無子曰獨。幼而無父曰孤。此四者，天下之窮民而無告者。文王發政施仁，必先斯四者。《詩》云：『哿矣富人，哀此煢獨。』」王曰：「善哉言乎！」
passages.translation_en: King Xuan of Qi asked, "Everyone tells me to tear down the Hall of Light. Should I tear it down or not?" Mencius replied, "The Hall of Light is the hall of a true king. If Your Majesty wishes to practice kingly government, then do not tear it down." The king said, "May I hear about kingly government?" Mencius replied, "In ancient times, when King Wen governed Qi, farmers were taxed one part in nine, descendants of officials received hereditary salaries, travelers were inspected at passes and markets but not taxed, fish traps at weirs were open to all, and the families of criminals were not punished for their crimes. The old and wifeless are called widowers. The old and husbandless are called widows. The old and childless are called the solitary. The young and fatherless are called orphans. These four are the most destitute people in the world, with no one to turn to. When King Wen put benevolent government into practice, he always gave priority to these four. The Odes say, 'The rich may get along, but pity those who are alone and desolate.'" The king said, "Well said!"

passages.text: 曰：「王如善之，則何為不行？」王曰：「寡人有疾，寡人好貨。」對曰：「昔者公劉好貨，《詩》云：『乃積乃倉，乃裹餱糧，于橐于囊。思戢用光。弓矢斯張，干戈戚揚，爰方啟行。』故居者有積倉，行者有裹糧也，然後可以爰方啟行。王如好貨，與百姓同之，於王何有？」王曰：「寡人有疾，寡人好色。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said, "If Your Majesty considers this good, then why not put it into practice?" The king said, "I have a weakness—I love wealth." Mencius replied, "In ancient times, Gongliu loved wealth. The Odes say, 'He piled up grain and stored provisions, he packed dried food in bags and sacks, thinking to unite and glorify his people. Bows and arrows were readied, shields and axes held aloft, and then he set forth on the march.' Thus those who stayed had full granaries, and those who marched had packed provisions—only then could he set forth on the march. If Your Majesty loves wealth but shares it with the people, what obstacle is there to kingly rule?" The king said, "I have a weakness—I love women."

passages.text: 對曰：「昔者大王好色，愛厥妃。《詩》云：『古公亶甫，來朝走馬，率西水滸，至于岐下。爰及姜女，聿來胥宇。』當是時也，內無怨女，外無曠夫。王如好色，與百姓同之，於王何有？」孟子謂齊宣王曰：「王之臣有託其妻子於其友，而之楚遊者。比其反也，則凍餒其妻子，則如之何？」王曰：「棄之。」曰：「士師不能治士，則如之何？」王曰：「已之。」曰：「四境之內不治，則如之何？」王顧左右而言他。
passages.translation_en: Mencius replied, "In ancient times, King Tai loved women and was devoted to his consort. The Odes say, 'Gugong Danfu came in the morning, riding his horse, following the banks of the western river, until he reached the foot of Mount Qi. He brought Lady Jiang along, and together they came to find a home.' In those times, there were no resentful women left unmarried at home, and no frustrated men left without wives. If Your Majesty loves women but shares this concern with the people, what obstacle is there to kingly rule?" Mencius said to King Xuan of Qi, "Suppose one of Your Majesty's ministers entrusted his wife and children to a friend and traveled to Chu. When he returned, he found that his friend had let his wife and children suffer cold and hunger. What should he do?" The king said, "Cast off that friend." Mencius said, "If the chief judge cannot keep order among his officers, what should be done?" The king said, "Dismiss him." Mencius said, "If the territory within the four borders is not well governed, what then?" The king looked left and right and changed the subject.

passages.text: 孟子見齊宣王曰：「所謂故國者，非謂有喬木之謂也，有世臣之謂也。王無親臣矣，昔者所進，今日不知其亡也。」王曰：「吾何以識其不才而舍之？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius had an audience with King Xuan of Qi and said, "What is meant by an 'established state' is not one that has tall trees, but one that has ministers whose families have served for generations. Your Majesty no longer has any trusted ministers. Those who were advanced in the past have disappeared, and you do not even know it." The king said, "How can I identify the incompetent and dismiss them?"

passages.text: 曰：「國君進賢，如不得已，將使卑踰尊，疏踰戚，可不慎與？左右皆曰賢，未可也；諸大夫皆曰賢，未可也；國人皆曰賢，然後察之；見賢焉，然後用之。左右皆曰不可，勿聽；諸大夫皆曰不可，勿聽；國人皆曰不可，然後察之；見不可焉，然後去之。左右皆曰可殺，勿聽；諸大夫皆曰可殺，勿聽；國人皆曰可殺，然後察之；見可殺焉，然後殺之。故曰，國人殺之也。如此，然後可以為民父母。」齊宣王問曰：「湯放桀，武王伐紂，有諸？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said, "When a ruler promotes the worthy, if he has no choice but to let the humble rise above the noble and the distant above the near, should he not be cautious? When those around you all say someone is worthy, that is not enough. When all the grandees say someone is worthy, that is not enough. When all the people of the state say someone is worthy, then examine the person; if you find them worthy, then employ them. When those around you all say someone is unfit, do not listen. When all the grandees say someone is unfit, do not listen. When all the people of the state say someone is unfit, then examine the person; if you find them unfit, then dismiss them. When those around you all say someone deserves death, do not listen. When all the grandees say someone deserves death, do not listen. When all the people of the state say someone deserves death, then examine the case; if you find they deserve death, then execute them. Thus it is said that the people of the state executed him. Only in this way can a ruler be a parent to the people." King Xuan of Qi asked, "Is it true that Tang banished Jie and that King Wu attacked Zhou?"

passages.text: 孟子對曰：「於傳有之。」曰：「臣弒其君可乎？」曰：「賊仁者謂之賊，賊義者謂之殘，殘賊之人謂之一夫。聞誅一夫紂矣，未聞弒君也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius replied, "So it says in the records." The king said, "Is it permissible for a minister to kill his sovereign?" Mencius said, "One who mutilates benevolence is called a mutilator. One who cripples righteousness is called a crippler. A mutilator and crippler is a mere fellow. I have heard of the execution of the mere fellow Zhou, but I have not heard of the killing of a sovereign."

passages.text: 孟子見齊宣王曰：「為巨室，則必使工師求大木。工師得大木。則王喜，以為能勝其任也。匠人斵而小之，則王怒，以為不勝其任矣。夫人幼而學之，壯而欲行之。王曰『姑舍女所學而從我』，則何如？今有璞玉於此，雖萬鎰，必使玉人彫琢之。至於治國家，則曰『姑舍女所學而從我』，則何以異於教玉人彫琢玉哉？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius had an audience with King Xuan of Qi and said, "If you are building a great mansion, you will surely have the master builder search for large timbers. When the master builder finds large timbers, Your Majesty will be pleased, thinking him capable of fulfilling his task. If the carpenters then whittle the timbers down too small, Your Majesty will be angry, thinking them unfit for the task. Now, a person studies something from youth and wishes to put it into practice in adulthood. If Your Majesty says, 'Set aside what you have learned and follow my way instead,' what would you think of that? Suppose there is a piece of uncut jade here worth a vast fortune. You would surely have a jade craftsman carve and polish it. Yet when it comes to governing the state, you say, 'Set aside what you have learned and follow my way instead.' How is this any different from trying to teach the jade craftsman how to carve jade?"

passages.text: 齊人伐燕，勝之。宣王問曰：「或謂寡人勿取，或謂寡人取之。以萬乘之國伐萬乘之國，五旬而舉之，人力不至於此。不取，必有天殃。取之，何如？」孟子對曰：「取之而燕民悅，則取之。古之人有行之者，武王是也。取之而燕民不悅，則勿取。古之人有行之者，文王是也。以萬乘之國伐萬乘之國，簞食壺漿，以迎王師。豈有他哉？避水火也。如水益深，如火益熱，亦運而已矣。」
passages.translation_en: The people of Qi attacked Yan and conquered it. King Xuan asked, "Some advise me not to annex it; others advise me to annex it. For a state of ten thousand chariots to attack another state of ten thousand chariots and conquer it in fifty days—human strength alone cannot account for this. If I do not annex it, there will surely be a calamity from Heaven. What do you think of annexing it?" Mencius replied, "If you annex it and the people of Yan are pleased, then annex it. Among the ancients, there was one who did this—King Wu. If you annex it and the people of Yan are not pleased, then do not annex it. Among the ancients, there was one who acted this way—King Wen. When a state of ten thousand chariots attacks another state of ten thousand chariots, and the people welcome the army with baskets of food and jars of drink, there is no other reason—they are fleeing from fire and flood. But if the water becomes even deeper and the fire even hotter, the people will simply turn elsewhere."

passages.text: 齊人伐燕，取之。諸侯將謀救燕。宣王曰：「諸侯多謀伐寡人者，何以待之？」孟子對曰：「臣聞七十里為政於天下者，湯是也。未聞以千里畏人者也。《書》曰：『湯一征，自葛始。』天下信之。『東面而征，西夷怨；南面而征，北狄怨。曰，奚為後我？』民望之，若大旱之望雲霓也。歸市者不止，耕者不變。誅其君而弔其民，若時雨降，民大悅。《書》曰：『徯我后，后來其蘇。』
passages.translation_en: The people of Qi attacked Yan and annexed it. The other feudal lords planned to rescue Yan. King Xuan said, "Many of the feudal lords are plotting to attack me. How should I deal with them?" Mencius replied, "I have heard of one who, with only seventy li of territory, brought order to the whole world—that was Tang. I have never heard of one who, with a thousand li of territory, lived in fear of others. The Documents say, 'Tang's campaigns began with Ge.' The whole world trusted him. 'When he marched east, the western tribes complained; when he marched south, the northern tribes complained, saying, Why does he put us last?' The people longed for him as people in a great drought long for clouds and rainbows. Those going to market were not delayed; those plowing the fields were not disturbed. He punished the rulers and comforted the people, and his coming was like timely rain. The people were overjoyed. The Documents say, 'We awaited our lord; when the lord comes, we shall be revived.'"

passages.text: 「今燕虐其民，王往而征之。民以為將拯己於水火之中也，簞食壺漿，以迎王師。若殺其父兄，係累其子弟，毀其宗廟，遷其重器，如之何其可也？天下固畏齊之彊也。今又倍地而不行仁政，是動天下之兵也。王速出令，反其旄倪，止其重器，謀於燕眾，置君而後去之，則猶可及止也。」鄒與魯鬨。穆公問曰：「吾有司死者三十三人，而民莫之死也。誅之，則不可勝誅；不誅，則疾視其長上之死而不救，如之何則可也？」
passages.translation_en: "Now Yan was oppressing its people, and Your Majesty went and punished it. The people thought you were going to rescue them from fire and flood, and they welcomed your army with baskets of food and jars of drink. But if you kill their fathers and elder brothers, put their sons and younger brothers in chains, destroy their ancestral temples, and carry off their precious vessels—how can that be acceptable? The world already fears the strength of Qi. Now you double your territory without practicing benevolent government—this will set the armies of the world in motion against you. I urge Your Majesty to issue orders at once: release the old and young captives, stop removing the precious vessels, consult with the people of Yan, install a new ruler, and then withdraw. If you do this, it may still be possible to avert disaster." There was a clash between Zou and Lu. Duke Mu asked, "Thirty-three of my officials were killed, and not a single commoner died to save them. If I punish the people, there are too many to punish. If I do not punish them, they simply looked on as their superiors were killed without lifting a hand. What should be done?"

passages.text: 孟子對曰：「凶年饑歲，君之民老弱轉乎溝壑，壯者散而之四方者，幾千人矣；而君之倉廩實，府庫充，有司莫以告，是上慢而殘下也。曾子曰：『戒之戒之！出乎爾者，反乎爾者也。』夫民今而後得反之也。君無尤焉。君行仁政，斯民親其上、死其長矣。」滕文公問曰：「滕，小國也，間於齊楚。事齊乎？事楚乎？」孟子對曰：「是謀非吾所能及也。無已，則有一焉：鑿斯池也，築斯城也，與民守之，效死而民弗去，則是可為也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius replied, "In years of famine and hardship, the old and weak among Your Lordship's people who ended up dead in ditches, and the able-bodied who scattered to the four directions, numbered in the thousands. Yet Your Lordship's granaries were full and your treasuries overflowing, and not a single official reported the crisis. This is for those above to be negligent and cruel to those below. Zengzi said, 'Beware, beware! What goes out from you will come back to you.' The people have now for the first time been able to repay what they received. Do not blame them, Your Lordship. If you practice benevolent government, the people will love their superiors and die for their leaders." Duke Wen of Teng asked, "Teng is a small state, wedged between Qi and Chu. Should I serve Qi, or should I serve Chu?" Mencius replied, "This is a question beyond my ability to answer. But if you insist, there is one course: dig your moats deeper, build your walls higher, and defend them together with your people. If the people would rather die than leave, then there is something worth doing."

passages.text: 滕文公問曰：「齊人將築薛，吾甚恐。如之何則可？」孟子對曰：「昔者大王居邠，狄人侵之，去之岐山之下居焉。非擇而取之，不得已也。苟為善，後世子孫必有王者矣。君子創業垂統，為可繼也。若夫成功，則天也。君如彼何哉？彊為善而已矣。」滕文公問曰：「滕，小國也。竭力以事大國，則不得免焉。如之何則可？」
passages.translation_en: Duke Wen of Teng asked, "Qi is going to fortify Xue. I am terrified. What should I do?" Mencius replied, "In ancient times, King Tai lived in Bin, and the Di tribes invaded. He left and settled at the foot of Mount Qi. He did not choose to do this—he had no alternative. If you do good, among your descendants in later generations there will surely be a true king. A gentleman founds a legacy and establishes a tradition that can be carried on. As for achieving success, that is up to Heaven. What can Your Lordship do about it? Simply strive to do good, that is all." Duke Wen of Teng asked, "Teng is a small state. We exhaust ourselves serving the great states, yet we still cannot avoid their demands. What should I do?"

passages.text: 孟子對曰：「昔者大王居邠，狄人侵之。事之以皮幣，不得免焉；事之以犬馬，不得免焉；事之以珠玉，不得免焉。乃屬其耆老而告之曰：『狄人之所欲者，吾土地也。吾聞之也：君子不以其所以養人者害人。二三子何患乎無君？我將去之。』去邠，踰梁山，邑于岐山之下居焉。邠人曰：『仁人也，不可失也。』從之者如歸市。或曰：『世守也，非身之所能為也。效死勿去。』君請擇於斯二者。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius replied, "In ancient times, King Tai lived in Bin, and the Di tribes invaded. He tried to buy them off with hides and silks, but could not avoid their demands. He tried to buy them off with dogs and horses, but could not avoid their demands. He tried to buy them off with pearls and jade, but could not avoid their demands. Then he gathered the elders and announced, 'What the Di people want is our land. I have heard it said: a gentleman does not use that which nourishes people to harm people. My friends, why should you worry about having no ruler? I shall leave.' He left Bin, crossed Mount Liang, and built a settlement at the foot of Mount Qi. The people of Bin said, 'He is a benevolent man. We must not lose him.' Those who followed him were like people flocking to market. Others said, 'This land has been guarded by our family for generations—it is not ours alone to abandon. We should defend it to the death.' Your Lordship, please choose between these two courses."

passages.text: 魯平公將出。嬖人臧倉者請曰：「他日君出，則必命有司所之。今乘輿已駕矣，有司未知所之。敢請。」公曰：「將見孟子。」曰：「何哉？君所為輕身以先於匹夫者，以為賢乎？禮義由賢者出。而孟子之後喪踰前喪。君無見焉！」公曰：「諾。」
passages.translation_en: Duke Ping of Lu was about to go out when his favorite attendant, Zang Cang, asked, "On other occasions when Your Lordship goes out, you always instruct the officials where you are going. The carriage is already harnessed, but the officials do not yet know the destination. May I ask where you are going?" The duke said, "I am going to see Mencius." Zang Cang said, "What is this? That you would lower yourself to call first on a commoner—is it because you consider him worthy? Propriety and righteousness come from the worthy. Yet Mencius's funeral for his mother exceeded his funeral for his father. I urge Your Lordship not to see him." The duke said, "Very well."

passages.text: 樂正子入見，曰：「君奚為不見孟軻也？」曰：「或告寡人曰，『孟子之後喪踰前喪』，是以不往見也。」曰：「何哉君所謂踰者？前以士，後以大夫；前以三鼎，而後以五鼎與？」曰：「否。謂棺槨衣衾之美也。」曰：「非所謂踰也，貧富不同也。」樂正子見孟子，曰：「克告於君，君為來見也。嬖人有臧倉者沮君，君是以不果來也。」曰：「行或使之，止或尼之。行止，非人所能也。吾之不遇魯侯，天也。臧氏之子焉能使予不遇哉？」
passages.translation_en: Yue Zhengzi went in to see the duke and said, "Why did Your Lordship not go to see Mencius?" The duke said, "Someone told me that Mencius's funeral for his mother exceeded his funeral for his father, and so I did not go." Yue Zhengzi said, "What do you mean by 'exceeded'? Do you mean that the first was conducted with the rites for a common officer and the second with those for a grandee? That the first used three sacrificial vessels and the second used five?" The duke said, "No. I meant the superior quality of the coffin, outer coffin, and burial garments." Yue Zhengzi said, "That is not 'exceeding'—it is simply the difference between being poor and being better off." Yue Zhengzi went to see Mencius and said, "I told the duke about you, and he was going to come see you. But one of his favorites, Zang Cang, dissuaded him, and so he did not come after all." Mencius said, "When a man acts, there is something that drives him forward; when he stops, there is something that holds him back. Whether he acts or stops is not entirely within human control. That I did not meet the Marquis of Lu was Heaven's doing. How could that fellow of the Zang family have kept me from meeting him?"

passages.text: 公孫丑問曰：「夫子當路於齊，管仲、晏子之功，可復許乎？」孟子曰：「子誠齊人也，知管仲、晏子而已矣。或問乎曾西曰；『吾子與子路孰賢？』曾西蹴然曰：『吾先子之所畏也。』曰：『然則吾子與管仲孰賢？』曾西艴然不悅，曰：『爾何曾比予於管仲？管仲得君，如彼其專也；行乎國政，如彼其久也；功烈，如彼其卑也。爾何曾比予於是？』」曰：「管仲，曾西之所不為也，而子為我願之乎？」
passages.translation_en: Gongsun Chou asked: "If you, Master, were given a position of power in Qi, could the achievements of Guan Zhong and Yan Zi be repeated?" Mencius replied: "You are truly a man of Qi—you know only of Guan Zhong and Yan Zi. Someone once asked Zeng Xi: 'Who is worthier, you or Zilu?' Zeng Xi said uneasily: 'Zilu was one whom my grandfather held in awe.' The questioner continued: 'Then who is worthier, you or Guan Zhong?' Zeng Xi grew visibly displeased and said: 'How dare you compare me to Guan Zhong! Guan Zhong enjoyed his lord's exclusive trust to such a degree; he administered the state for so long; and yet his accomplishments were so modest. How dare you compare me to him?'" Mencius then said: "Guan Zhong was someone Zeng Xi would never deign to be—and yet you would wish me to be like him?"

passages.text: 曰：「管仲以其君霸，晏子以其君顯。管仲、晏子猶不足為與？」曰：「以齊王，由反手也。」曰：「若是，則弟子之惑滋甚。且以文王之德，百年而後崩，猶未洽於天下；武王、周公繼之，然後大行。今言王若易然，則文王不足法與？」
passages.translation_en: Gongsun Chou said: "Guan Zhong made his lord a hegemon, and Yan Zi made his lord illustrious. Are Guan Zhong and Yan Zi still not worthy models?" Mencius replied: "To make Qi a true king would be as easy as turning over one's hand." Gongsun Chou said: "If so, then your disciple is even more confused. King Wen, with all his virtue, lived to be nearly a hundred before he died, and still his influence had not permeated all under Heaven. It took King Wu and the Duke of Zhou to carry on his work before it was fully realized. Now you speak of true kingship as if it were easy—does that mean King Wen is not worth emulating?"

passages.text: 曰：「文王何可當也？由湯至於武丁，賢聖之君六七作。天下歸殷久矣，久則難變也。武丁朝諸侯有天下，猶運之掌也。紂之去武丁未久也，其故家遺俗，流風善政，猶有存者；又有微子、微仲、王子比干、箕子、膠鬲皆賢人也，相與輔相之，故久而後失之也。尺地莫非其有也，一民莫非其臣也，然而文王猶方百里起，是以難也。齊人有言曰：『雖有智慧，不如乘勢；雖有鎡基，不如待時。』
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "How can anyone be compared to King Wen? From Tang to Wu Ding, there arose six or seven worthy and sagely rulers. The world had belonged to the Yin dynasty for a long time, and what has lasted long is hard to change. Wu Ding held court over all the lords and possessed the empire as easily as turning it in his palm. The tyrant Zhou was not far removed from Wu Ding's time—the old families and inherited customs, the lingering influence of good governance, still survived. Moreover, there were the Viscount of Wei, Zhong of Wei, Prince Bi Gan, the Viscount of Ji, and Jiao Ge—all worthy men who assisted the dynasty together. So it was a long time before the dynasty was lost. Every foot of land belonged to Yin, every person was its subject—and yet King Wen had to rise from a territory of only a hundred li. That is why it was so difficult. The people of Qi have a saying: 'Though you have wisdom, it is better to ride the momentum of circumstances; though you have good tools, it is better to wait for the right season.'"

passages.text: 「今時則易然也。夏后、殷、周之盛，地未有過千里者也，而齊有其地矣；雞鳴狗吠相聞，而達乎四境，而齊有其民矣。地不改辟矣，民不改聚矣，行仁政而王，莫之能禦也。且王者之不作，未有疏於此時者也；民之憔悴於虐政，未有甚於此時者也。飢者易為食，渴者易為飲。孔子曰：『德之流行，速於置郵而傳命。』當今之時，萬乘之國行仁政，民之悅之，猶解倒懸也。故事半古之人，功必倍之，惟此時為然。」
passages.translation_en: "The present time, however, makes it easy. At the height of the Xia, Yin, and Zhou dynasties, none possessed territory exceeding a thousand li—yet Qi already has that much land. The sounds of roosters crowing and dogs barking can be heard all the way to its four borders—Qi already has that many people. The land need not be further opened, the people need not be further gathered: simply practice benevolent government and become a true king—no one can prevent it. Moreover, never has there been a longer gap without a true king arising than now; never have the people suffered more bitterly under cruel government than now. The hungry are easy to feed; the thirsty are easy to give drink. Confucius said: 'The spread of virtue is swifter than the relay of royal commands by post.' In our present age, if a state of ten thousand chariots were to practice benevolent government, the people's joy would be like being released from hanging upside down. Therefore, with half the effort of the ancients, one can achieve double the results—only this moment in time makes that possible."

passages.text: 公孫丑問曰：「夫子加齊之卿相，得行道焉，雖由此霸王不異矣。如此，則動心否乎？」孟子曰：「否。我四十不動心。」曰：「若是，則夫子過孟賁遠矣。」曰：「是不難，告子先我不動心。」曰：「不動心有道乎？」
passages.translation_en: Gongsun Chou asked: "If you, Master, were made chief minister of Qi and could put your Way into practice, it would not be surprising if this led to hegemony or true kingship. In such a case, would your heart be moved?" Mencius replied: "No. Since the age of forty, my heart has been unmoved." Gongsun Chou said: "If so, then you far surpass Meng Ben." Mencius said: "That is not difficult—Gaozi achieved an unmoved heart before I did." Gongsun Chou asked: "Is there a method for attaining an unmoved heart?"

passages.text: 曰：「有。北宮黝之養勇也，不膚撓，不目逃，思以一豪挫於人，若撻之於市朝。不受於褐寬博，亦不受於萬乘之君。視刺萬乘之君，若刺褐夫。無嚴諸侯。惡聲至，必反之。孟施舍之所養勇也，曰：『視不勝猶勝也。量敵而後進，慮勝而後會，是畏三軍者也。舍豈能為必勝哉？能無懼而已矣。』孟施舍似曾子，北宮黝似子夏。夫二子之勇，未知其孰賢，然而孟施舍守約也。昔者曾子謂子襄曰：『子好勇乎？吾嘗聞大勇於夫子矣：自反而不縮，雖褐寬博，吾不惴焉；自反而縮，雖千萬人，吾往矣。』孟施舍之守氣，又不如曾子之守約也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "There is. Beigong You cultivated courage in this way: he would not flinch in his skin nor avert his eyes. He regarded the slightest insult from anyone as equivalent to being flogged in the public square. What he would not accept from a common man in coarse cloth, he would equally not accept from the lord of ten thousand chariots. He would as readily stab the lord of ten thousand chariots as stab a common man. He stood in awe of no feudal lord—if harsh words came his way, he always returned them. Meng Shishe cultivated courage differently, saying: 'I regard defeat the same as victory. To size up the enemy before advancing, to calculate victory before engaging—that is to be intimidated by opposing armies. How could I guarantee victory? I can only be free of fear.' Meng Shishe resembled Master Zeng, while Beigong You resembled Zixia. As for which of the two was superior in courage, I cannot say—but Meng Shishe held to what was essential. In former times, Master Zeng said to Zixiang: 'Do you admire courage? I once heard about great courage from the Master: If upon self-examination I find I am not in the right, then even against a common man in coarse cloth, I would feel dread. But if upon self-examination I find I am in the right, then even against thousands and tens of thousands, I shall go forward.' Yet Meng Shishe's guarding of his vital energy still falls short of Master Zeng's holding to what is essential."

passages.text: 曰：「敢問夫子之不動心，與告子之不動心，可得聞與？」「告子曰：『不得於言，勿求於心；不得於心，勿求於氣。』不得於心，勿求於氣，可；不得於言，勿求於心，不可。夫志，氣之帥也；氣，體之充也。夫志至焉，氣次焉。故曰：『持其志，無暴其氣。』」「既曰『志至焉，氣次焉』，又曰『持其志無暴其氣』者，何也？」曰：「志壹則動氣，氣壹則動志也。今夫蹶者趨者，是氣也，而反動其心。」「敢問夫子惡乎長？」
passages.translation_en: Gongsun Chou asked: "May I ask about the difference between your unmoved heart, Master, and Gaozi's unmoved heart?" Mencius said: "Gaozi said: 'If you do not succeed with words, do not seek it in the heart; if you do not succeed with the heart, do not seek it in the vital energy.' Not to seek in vital energy what you cannot attain in the heart—that is acceptable. But not to seek in the heart what you cannot attain with words—that is unacceptable. The will is the commander of the vital energy; the vital energy fills the body. The will is paramount, and the vital energy comes next. Therefore I say: 'Hold firm to your will, and do not abuse your vital energy.'" Gongsun Chou asked: "You say the will is paramount and the vital energy comes next, yet you also say to hold firm to your will and not abuse your vital energy—why is that?" Mencius said: "When the will is concentrated, it moves the vital energy; when the vital energy is concentrated, it moves the will. For instance, stumbling and hurrying are matters of the vital energy, yet they in turn agitate the heart." Gongsun Chou asked: "May I ask where your particular strength lies, Master?"

passages.text: 曰：「我知言，我善養吾浩然之氣。」「敢問何謂浩然之氣？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "I understand words, and I am skilled at cultivating my flood-like vital energy." Gongsun Chou asked: "What do you mean by flood-like vital energy?"

passages.text: 曰：「難言也。其為氣也，至大至剛，以直養而無害，則塞于天地之閒。其為氣也，配義與道；無是，餒也。是集義所生者，非義襲而取之也。行有不慊於心，則餒矣。我故曰，告子未嘗知義，以其外之也。必有事焉而勿正，心勿忘，勿助長也。無若宋人然：宋人有閔其苗之不長而揠之者，芒芒然歸。謂其人曰：『今日病矣，予助苗長矣。』其子趨而往視之，苗則槁矣。天下之不助苗長者寡矣。以為無益而舍之者，不耘苗者也；助之長者，揠苗者也。非徒無益，而又害之。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "It is difficult to describe. As vital energy, it is supremely great and supremely strong. If nourished with uprightness and not harmed, it fills the space between Heaven and Earth. As vital energy, it is the companion of righteousness and the Way; without these, it starves. It is born from the accumulation of righteous deeds—it cannot be seized through occasional acts of righteousness. If one's conduct leaves anything that dissatisfies the heart, the energy starves. That is why I say Gaozi never understood righteousness—because he treated it as something external. One must work at it, but without forcing a predetermined result. The heart must not forget it, yet must not try to help it grow. Do not be like the man of Song: A man of Song was worried that his seedlings were not growing, so he pulled them up. He returned home looking drained and said to his family: 'I am exhausted today—I have been helping the seedlings grow.' His son rushed out to look, and the seedlings had all withered. Those in the world who do not try to help their seedlings grow are few. Those who abandon the effort as useless are like those who do not weed their seedlings. Those who try to help them grow are like those who pull up the seedlings—not merely useless, but positively harmful."

passages.text: 「何謂知言？」曰：「詖辭知其所蔽，淫辭知其所陷，邪辭知其所離，遁辭知其所窮。生於其心，害於其政；發於其政，害於其事。聖人復起，必從吾言矣。」「宰我、子貢善為說辭，冉牛、閔子、顏淵善言德行。孔子兼之，曰：『我於辭命則不能也。』然則夫子既聖矣乎？」
passages.translation_en: Gongsun Chou asked: "What do you mean by 'understanding words'?" Mencius said: "When words are one-sided, I can see what they obscure. When words are excessive, I can see the trap they have fallen into. When words are deviant, I can see how they have departed from the truth. When words are evasive, I can see the desperation behind them. When such distortions arise in a person's mind, they damage his governance; when they manifest in his governance, they damage his undertakings. Were a sage to arise again, he would surely agree with my words." Gongsun Chou said: "Zai Wo and Zigong excelled at rhetoric; Ran Niu, Min Zi, and Yan Hui excelled at virtuous conduct. Confucius combined both abilities, yet said: 'When it comes to rhetoric, I am not capable.' Does this mean you are already a sage, Master?"

passages.text: 曰：「惡！是何言也？昔者子貢、問於孔子曰：『夫子聖矣乎？』孔子曰：『聖則吾不能，我學不厭而教不倦也。』子貢曰：『學不厭，智也；教不倦，仁也。仁且智，夫子既聖矣！』夫聖，孔子不居，是何言也？」「昔者竊聞之：子夏、子游、子張皆有聖人之一體，冉牛、閔子、顏淵則具體而微。敢問所安。」曰：「姑舍是。」曰：「伯夷、伊尹何如？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "Good heavens! What are you saying? Once Zigong asked Confucius: 'Master, are you a sage?' Confucius replied: 'A sage I cannot claim to be. I am simply one who never tires of learning and never wearies of teaching.' Zigong said: 'Never tiring of learning—that is wisdom. Never wearying of teaching—that is benevolence. Possessing both benevolence and wisdom, you are already a sage, Master!' If sagehood was something even Confucius would not claim for himself, what kind of talk is this?" Gongsun Chou said: "I have heard it said that Zixia, Ziyou, and Zizhang each possessed one aspect of the sage, while Ran Niu, Min Zi, and Yan Hui possessed the whole but in lesser degree. May I ask where you place yourself?" Mencius said: "Let us set that question aside for now." Gongsun Chou asked: "What about Bo Yi and Yi Yin?"

passages.text: 曰：「不同道。非其君不事，非其民不使；治則進，亂則退，伯夷也。何事非君，何使非民；治亦進，亂亦進，伊尹也。可以仕則仕，可以止則止，可以久則久，可以速則速，孔子也。皆古聖人也，吾未能有行焉；乃所願，則學孔子也。」「伯夷、伊尹於孔子，若是班乎？」曰：「否。自有生民以來，未有孔子也。」曰：「然則有同與？」曰：「有。得百里之地而君之，皆能以朝諸侯有天下。行一不義、殺一不辜而得天下，皆不為也。是則同。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "Their ways were different. Bo Yi would serve no lord who was not his ideal, and would employ no people who were not his ideal; he advanced when there was good order and withdrew when there was chaos. Yi Yin said: 'Whom may I not serve as lord? Whom may I not employ as subjects?' He advanced in times of order and also advanced in times of chaos. Confucius would serve when it was appropriate to serve, would stop when it was appropriate to stop, would stay long when it was appropriate to stay, and would leave quickly when it was appropriate to leave. All three were ancient sages. I have not yet been able to practice what any of them did, but what I aspire to is to learn from Confucius." Gongsun Chou asked: "Are Bo Yi and Yi Yin in the same class as Confucius?" Mencius said: "No. Since the beginning of humankind, there has never been another Confucius." Gongsun Chou asked: "Then did they share anything in common?" Mencius said: "Yes. If given a territory of a hundred li to rule, they could all have brought the feudal lords to court and possessed the empire. And if it required committing a single unjust act or killing a single innocent person to gain the empire, none of them would have done it. In this they were the same."

passages.text: 曰：「敢問其所以異？」曰：「宰我、子貢、有若智足以知聖人。汙，不至阿其所好。宰我曰：『以予觀於夫子，賢於堯舜遠矣。』子貢曰：『見其禮而知其政，聞其樂而知其德。由百世之後，等百世之王，莫之能違也。自生民以來，未有夫子也。』有若曰：『豈惟民哉？麒麟之於走獸，鳳凰之於飛鳥，太山之於丘垤，河海之於行潦，類也。聖人之於民，亦類也。出於其類，拔乎其萃，自生民以來，未有盛於孔子也。』」
passages.translation_en: Gongsun Chou asked: "May I ask in what way they differed?" Mencius said: "Zai Wo, Zigong, and You Ruo were wise enough to recognize a sage. Even in their partiality, they would not stoop to flattering the one they admired. Zai Wo said: 'In my observation, the Master far surpasses Yao and Shun.' Zigong said: 'By seeing a state's rituals, one can know its governance; by hearing its music, one can know its virtue. Looking back over a hundred generations, one can assess a hundred generations of kings—and none can be found to contradict this. Since the beginning of humankind, there has never been anyone like the Master.' You Ruo said: 'Is it only among humans? The unicorn is to running beasts, the phoenix is to flying birds, Mount Tai is to small hills, the rivers and seas are to puddles—they are all of the same kind, yet stand far above. The sage is to the people what these are—of the same kind, yet towering above the rest. Since the beginning of humankind, there has never been one greater than Confucius.'"

passages.text: 孟子曰：「以力假仁者霸，霸必有大國，以德行仁者王，王不待大。湯以七十里，文王以百里。以力服人者，非心服也，力不贍也；以德服人者，中心悅而誠服也，如七十子之服孔子也。《詩》云：『自西自東，自南自北，無思不服。』此之謂也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "One who uses force while feigning benevolence is a hegemon—a hegemon must have a large state. One who practices benevolence through virtue is a true king—a true king need not have a large state. Tang became king with only seventy li, King Wen with only a hundred li. One who subdues people by force does not win their hearts—they submit because their own strength is insufficient. One who wins people through virtue gains their heartfelt and sincere submission, as the seventy disciples submitted to Confucius. The Odes say: 'From west and east, from south and north, none thought of not submitting.' This is what it means."

passages.text: 孟子曰：「仁則榮，不仁則辱。今惡辱而居不仁，是猶惡溼而居下也。如惡之，莫如貴德而尊士，賢者在位，能者在職。國家閒暇，及是時明其政刑。雖大國，必畏之矣。《詩》云：『迨天之未陰雨，徹彼桑土，綢繆牖戶。今此下民，或敢侮予？』孔子曰：『為此詩者，其知道乎！能治其國家，誰敢侮之？』今國家閒暇，及是時般樂怠敖，是自求禍也。禍褔無不自己求之者。《詩》云：『永言配命，自求多褔。』《太甲》曰：『天作孽，猶可違；自作孽，不可活。』此之謂也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "Benevolence brings glory; the lack of benevolence brings disgrace. To hate disgrace while dwelling in unbenevolence is like hating dampness while living in a low-lying place. If one truly hates it, the best course is to honor virtue and respect the worthy: place the virtuous in positions of authority and the capable in office. When the state is at peace, use that time to clarify its governance and laws. Then even great states will stand in awe. The Odes say: 'Before the sky clouds over with rain, I strip the bark from mulberry roots and bind tight my windows and doors. Now you people below—who would dare insult me?' Confucius said: 'Whoever composed this poem truly understood the Way! If one can govern his state well, who would dare insult him?' But now, when states are at peace, rulers use the time for idle pleasure and lazy indulgence—this is to invite disaster upon themselves. Misfortune and fortune are never anything but what one brings upon oneself. The Odes say: 'Ever strive to accord with Heaven's mandate, and seek for yourself abundant blessings.' The Taijia says: 'When Heaven sends down calamities, one may still escape them; when one brings calamity upon oneself, there is no surviving it.' This is what it means."

passages.text: 孟子曰：「尊賢使能，俊傑在位，則天下之士皆悅而願立於其朝矣。市廛而不征，法而不廛，則天下之商皆悅而願藏於其市矣。關譏而不征，則天下之旅皆悅而願出於其路矣。耕者助而不稅，則天下之農皆悅而願耕於其野矣。廛無夫里之布，則天下之民皆悅而願為之氓矣。信能行此五者，則鄰國之民仰之若父母矣。率其子弟，攻其父母，自生民以來，未有能濟者也。如此，則無敵於天下。無敵於天下者，天吏也。然而不王者，未之有也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "If you honor the worthy and employ the capable, placing outstanding men in office, then all the scholars in the world will be delighted and will wish to serve at your court. If in the marketplace you charge rent on stalls but do not tax the goods, or enforce regulations but do not charge rent, then all the merchants in the world will be delighted and will wish to store their goods in your markets. If at the border passes you inspect travelers but do not tax them, then all the travelers in the world will be delighted and will wish to travel your roads. If farmers are asked only for communal labor and not taxed on their harvest, then all the farmers in the world will be delighted and will wish to till your fields. If there are no additional levies on households, then all the people in the world will be delighted and will wish to become your subjects. If you can truly carry out these five things, then the people of neighboring states will look up to you as a parent. To lead their own children to attack their parent—since the beginning of humankind, no one has ever succeeded at this. In this way, you will be without rival in the world. One who is without rival in the world is an agent of Heaven. Having all this yet failing to become a true king—that has never happened."

passages.text: 孟子曰：「人皆有不忍人之心。先王有不忍人之心，斯有不忍人之政矣。以不忍人之心，行不忍人之政，治天下可運之掌上。所以謂人皆有不忍人之心者，今人乍見孺子將入於井，皆有怵惕惻隱之心。非所以內交於孺子之父母也，非所以要譽於鄉黨朋友也，非惡其聲而然也。由是觀之，無惻隱之心，非人也；無羞惡之心，非人也；無辭讓之心，非人也；無是非之心，非人也。惻隱之心，仁之端也；羞惡之心，義之端也；辭讓之心，禮之端也；是非之心，智之端也。人之有是四端也，猶其有四體也。有是四端而自謂不能者，自賊者也；謂其君不能者，賊其君者也。凡有四端於我者，知皆擴而充之矣，若火之始然，泉之始達。苟能充之，足以保四海；苟不充之，不足以事父母。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "All people have a heart that cannot bear the suffering of others. The former kings had hearts that could not bear the suffering of others, and so they had governments that could not bear the suffering of others. If one governs the world with a heart that cannot bear suffering, the world can be managed as easily as turning something in one's palm. The reason I say all people have a heart that cannot bear the suffering of others is this: Suppose someone suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well. Everyone would feel alarm and compassion—not because they seek to gain favor with the child's parents, not because they seek praise from neighbors and friends, and not because they dislike the sound of the child's cries. From this we can see: one who lacks the feeling of compassion is not human; one who lacks the feeling of shame is not human; one who lacks the feeling of deference is not human; one who lacks the sense of right and wrong is not human. The feeling of compassion is the sprout of benevolence; the feeling of shame is the sprout of righteousness; the feeling of deference is the sprout of propriety; the sense of right and wrong is the sprout of wisdom. People have these four sprouts just as they have four limbs. For one who has these four sprouts to say he cannot develop them is to cripple himself; to say his ruler cannot develop them is to cripple his ruler. Since everyone possesses these four sprouts within, let all know to expand and fulfill them. They are like a fire just beginning to burn, a spring just beginning to flow. If one can fulfill them, they are sufficient to protect all within the four seas; if one fails to fulfill them, they will not even be sufficient to serve one's parents."

passages.text: 孟子曰：「矢人豈不仁於函人哉？矢人唯恐不傷人，函人唯恐傷人。巫匠亦然，故術不可不慎也。孔子曰：『里仁為美。擇不處仁，焉得智？』夫仁，天之尊爵也，人之安宅也。莫之禦而不仁，是不智也。不仁、不智、無禮、無義，人役也。人役而恥為役，由弓人而恥為弓，矢人而恥為矢也。如恥之，莫如為仁。仁者如射，射者正己而後發。發而不中，不怨勝己者，反求諸己而已矣。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "Is the arrow-maker really less benevolent than the armor-maker? The arrow-maker's only fear is that his arrows will not harm people; the armor-maker's only fear is that people will be harmed. The same is true of the healer and the coffin-maker. Therefore, one must be careful in choosing one's profession. Confucius said: 'It is beautiful to dwell among the benevolent. If one chooses not to dwell among the benevolent, how can one be considered wise?' Benevolence is Heaven's most honored rank and the most secure dwelling of humankind. When nothing prevents one from being benevolent and yet one is not—this is a lack of wisdom. One who is neither benevolent, nor wise, nor observant of propriety, nor righteous—such a person is a slave. To be a slave and feel ashamed of being a slave is like being a bow-maker who is ashamed of making bows, or an arrow-maker who is ashamed of making arrows. If one truly feels the shame, the best course is to practice benevolence. The benevolent person is like an archer: the archer first corrects his own posture, then lets fly. If the arrow misses the mark, he does not resent those who surpassed him but turns inward to examine himself."

passages.text: 孟子曰：「子路，人告之以有過則喜。禹聞善言則拜。大舜有大焉，善與人同。舍己從人，樂取於人以為善。自耕、稼、陶、漁以至為帝，無非取於人者。取諸人以為善，是與人為善者也。故君子莫大乎與人為善。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "When someone pointed out a fault to Zilu, he was delighted. When Yu heard good counsel, he bowed in gratitude. The great Shun surpassed them both: he took goodness as something to share with others. He set aside his own ways to follow others, and delighted in learning from others in order to do good. From the time he was a farmer, a potter, and a fisherman, all the way until he became emperor, there was nothing he did not learn from others. To take from others in order to do good—this is to help others do good. Therefore, there is no greater thing for a noble person than to help others do good."

passages.text: 孟子曰：「伯夷，非其君不事，非其友不友。不立於惡人之朝，不與惡人言。立於惡人之朝，與惡人言，如以朝衣朝冠坐於塗炭。推惡惡之心，思與鄉人立，其冠不正，望望然去之，若將浼焉。是故諸侯雖有善其辭命而至者，不受也。不受也者，是亦不屑就已。柳下惠，不羞汙君，不卑小官。進不隱賢，必以其道。遺佚而不怨，阨窮而不憫。故曰：『爾為爾，我為我，雖袒裼裸裎於我側，爾焉能浼我哉？』故由由然與之偕而不自失焉，援而止之而止。援而止之而止者，是亦不屑去已。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "Bo Yi would serve no lord who was not his ideal and befriend no one who was not his ideal. He would not stand in the court of a wicked man, nor would he speak with a wicked man. To stand in such a court or speak with such a man would be, to him, like sitting in court robes and court cap amidst mud and coals. Extending this hatred of wickedness, if he stood beside a villager whose cap was crooked, he would turn away in disgust as if he might be defiled. For this reason, even when feudal lords came with polite invitations, he would refuse them. He refused because he disdained to go to them. Liu Xia Hui, on the other hand, was not ashamed to serve a corrupt lord and did not consider a minor office beneath him. When advanced, he did not conceal his talents, but always acted according to his principles. When overlooked and left in obscurity, he did not complain; when reduced to poverty, he did not grieve. He said: 'You are you and I am I. Even if you were to stand naked beside me, how could you defile me?' So he was content to remain in their company without losing himself. When they pulled at him to stay, he stayed—he stayed because he did not deign to leave."

passages.text: 孟子曰：「伯夷隘，柳下惠不恭。隘與不恭，君子不由也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "Bo Yi was too narrow; Liu Xia Hui was too lacking in respect. The noble person follows neither extreme."

passages.text: 孟子曰：「天時不如地利，地利不如人和。三里之城，七里之郭，環而攻之而不勝。夫環而攻之，必有得天時者矣；然而不勝者，是天時不如地利也。城非不高也，池非不深也，兵革非不堅利也，米粟非不多也；委而去之，是地利不如人和也。故曰：域民不以封疆之界，固國不以山谿之險，威天下不以兵革之利。得道者多助，失道者寡助。寡助之至，親戚畔之；多助之至，天下順之。以天下之所順，攻親戚之所畔；故君子有不戰，戰必勝矣。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "Favorable weather is not as good as advantageous terrain, and advantageous terrain is not as good as unity among the people. A city wall of three li, with outer walls of seven li, may be surrounded and attacked yet not taken. To surround and attack it, the attackers must have had favorable weather; yet they still could not win — this shows that favorable weather is not as good as advantageous terrain. When the city walls are not low, the moats not shallow, the weapons and armor not poor, the grain supplies not scarce — yet the defenders abandon it all and flee — this shows that advantageous terrain is not as good as unity among the people. Therefore it is said: Confining the people does not depend on borders and boundaries; securing the state does not depend on mountains and rivers; overawing the world does not depend on military might. He who has the Way finds many allies; he who lacks the Way finds few. When allies are fewest, even one's own relatives turn away; when allies are most numerous, the whole world submits. When one who commands the world's allegiance attacks one whose own kin have turned against him — therefore the gentleman either does not fight at all, or when he fights, he is certain to win."

passages.text: 孟子將朝王，王使人來曰：「寡人如就見者也，有寒疾，不可以風。朝將視朝，不識可使寡人得見乎？」對曰：「不幸而有疾，不能造朝。」明日，出吊於東郭氏，公孫丑曰：「昔者辭以病，今日吊，或者不可乎！」曰：「昔者疾，今日愈，如之何不吊？」王使人問疾，醫來。孟仲子對曰：「昔者有王命，有采薪之憂，不能造朝。今病小愈，趨造於朝，我不識能至否乎？」使數人要於路，曰：「請必無歸，而造於朝！」
passages.translation_en: Mencius was about to go to court to see the king. The king sent a messenger saying: "I would have liked to come see you, but I have a chill and cannot go out in the wind. Tomorrow morning I will hold court — may I see you then?" Mencius replied: "Unfortunately I too am ill and cannot go to court." The next day he went out to offer condolences at the Dongguo household. Gongsun Chou said: "Yesterday you excused yourself on account of illness, and today you go out to pay a condolence call — isn't that perhaps improper?" Mencius said: "Yesterday I was ill; today I have recovered. Why shouldn't I pay a condolence call?" The king sent someone to inquire after his illness, and a physician came. Meng Zhongzi replied on his behalf: "Yesterday he received the king's summons, but had a slight ailment and could not go to court. Today he is somewhat better and has hurried to court — I do not know whether he has arrived yet." He then sent several men to intercept Mencius on the road, saying: "Please, you absolutely must not go home — go to court!"

passages.text: 不得已而之景丑氏宿焉。景子曰：「內則父子，外則君臣，人之大倫也。父子主恩，君臣主敬。丑見王之敬子也，未見所以敬王也。」曰：「惡！是何言也！齊人無以仁義與王言者，豈以仁義為不美也？其心曰『是何足與言仁義也』云爾，則不敬莫大乎是。我非堯舜之道，不敢以陳於王前，故齊人莫如我敬王也。」景子曰：「否，非此之謂也。禮曰：『父召，無諾；君命召，不俟駕。』固將朝也，聞王命而遂不果，宜與夫禮若不相似然。」
passages.translation_en: Having no choice, Mencius went to stay at the Jingchou household. Master Jing said: "Within the family there is the bond of father and son; outside there is the bond of ruler and minister — these are the great relationships of human life. Between father and son, affection is paramount; between ruler and minister, respect is paramount. I have seen the king show respect to you, but I have not seen how you show respect to the king." Mencius said: "What! What kind of talk is this? Among the people of Qi, no one speaks to the king about benevolence and righteousness. Do you think it is because they consider benevolence and righteousness not admirable? In their hearts they think, 'This king is not worth talking to about benevolence and righteousness' — that is all. There is no greater disrespect than that. As for me, I would not dare present anything before the king that was not the Way of Yao and Shun. Therefore no one in Qi respects the king as much as I do." Master Jing said: "No, that is not what I meant. The rites say: 'When a father summons, do not answer merely yes; when a ruler commands your presence, do not wait for the carriage.' You were about to go to court, but upon hearing the king's summons you did not follow through — this seems inconsistent with propriety."

passages.text: 曰：「豈謂是與？曾子曰：『晉楚之富，不可及也。彼以其富，我以吾仁；彼以其爵，我以吾義，吾何慊乎哉？』夫豈不義而曾子言之？是或一道也。天下有達尊三：爵一，齒一，德一。朝廷莫如爵，鄉黨莫如齒，輔世長民莫如德。惡得有其一，以慢其二哉？故將大有為之君，必有所不召之臣。欲有謀焉，則就之。其尊德樂道，不如是不足與有為也。故湯之於伊尹，學焉而後臣之，故不勞而王；桓公之於管仲，學焉而後臣之，故不勞而霸。今天下地醜德齊，莫能相尚。無他，好臣其所教，而不好臣其所受教。湯之於伊尹，桓公之於管仲，則不敢召。管仲且猶不可召，而況不為管仲者乎？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "Is that really the point? Zengzi said: 'The wealth of Jin and Chu is beyond my reach. They have their wealth; I have my benevolence. They have their rank; I have my righteousness. What do I lack?' Surely Zengzi would not have said this if it were not right — it must represent one valid principle. In the world there are three things universally honored: rank, age, and virtue. At court, nothing compares to rank; in the village, nothing compares to age; for governing the world and leading the people, nothing compares to virtue. How can one who possesses only one of these look down upon the other two? Therefore a ruler who intends to accomplish great things must have ministers he does not summon. When he wishes to consult them, he goes to them. If his reverence for virtue and delight in the Way does not reach this level, he is not worth working with. Thus Tang first learned from Yi Yin, and only then made him a minister — and so he became king without difficulty. Duke Huan first learned from Guan Zhong, and only then made him a minister — and so he became hegemon without difficulty. Now the states are similar in territory and equal in virtue, and none can rise above the others. For no other reason than this: they prefer to make ministers of those they can instruct, not those from whom they can learn. Tang would not have dared summon Yi Yin, nor Duke Huan summon Guan Zhong. If even Guan Zhong could not be summoned, how much less one who would not stoop to be a Guan Zhong?"

passages.text: 陳臻問曰：「前日於齊，王餽兼金一百而不受；於宋，餽七十鎰而受；於薛，餽五十鎰而受。前日之不受是，則今日之受非也；今日之受是，則前日之不受非也。夫子必居一於此矣。」孟子曰：「皆是也。當在宋也，予將有遠行。行者必以贐，辭曰：『餽贐。』予何為不受？當在薛也，予有戒心。辭曰：『聞戒。』故為兵餽之，予何為不受？若於齊，則未有處也。無處而餽之，是貨之也。焉有君子而可以貨取乎？」
