It is not that Heaven has endowed them differently—it is because of what has drowned and sunk their hearts. Consider barley: sow the seeds and cover them. If the soil is the same and the planting time is the same, the plants shoot up vigorously and by the summer solstice they have all ripened. If there are differences, it is because of variations in the richness of the soil, the nourishment of rain and dew, and the unevenness of human effort. Therefore, all things of the same kind are similar to one another. Why should we doubt this only when it comes to human beings? The sage and I are of the same kind. Thus Longzi said: 'If someone makes sandals without knowing the foot, I know he will not make baskets.' Sandals resemble one another because all feet in the world are alike. With regard to taste, all mouths have the same preferences. Yi Ya was simply the first to discover what our mouths prefer. If each person's sense of taste were as different from others' as dogs and horses are different from us, then why would the whole world follow Yi Ya's judgments about flavor? In matters of taste, the whole world looks to Yi Ya—this shows that all mouths in the world are alike. It is the same with the ear. In matters of music, the whole world looks to Music Master Kuang—this shows that all ears in the world are alike. It is the same with the eye. As for Zidu, no one in the world did not recognize his handsomeness. Anyone who did not recognize Zidu's handsomeness had no eyes. Therefore I say: mouths have the same preferences in taste; ears have the same preferences in sound; eyes have the same preferences in beauty. When it comes to the heart alone, is there nothing that all share? What the heart shares in common is principle and righteousness. The sage simply discovered first what our hearts share in common. Therefore principle and righteousness please our hearts just as grain-fed meat pleases our mouths."

passages.text: 孟子曰：「牛山之木嘗美矣，以其郊於大國也，斧斤伐之，可以為美乎？是其日夜之所息，雨露之所潤，非無萌櫱之生焉，牛羊又從而牧之，是以若彼濯濯也。人見其濯濯也，以為未嘗有材焉，此豈山之性也哉？雖存乎人者，豈無仁義之心哉？其所以放其良心者，亦猶斧斤之於木也，旦旦而伐之，可以為美乎？其日夜之所息，平旦之氣，其好惡與人相近也者幾希，則其旦晝之所為，有梏亡之矣。梏之反覆，則其夜氣不足以存；夜氣不足以存，則其違禽獸不遠矣。人見其禽獸也，而以為未嘗有才焉者，是豈人之情也哉？故苟得其養，無物不長；苟失其養，無物不消。孔子曰：『操則存，舍則亡；出入無時，莫知其鄉。』惟心之謂與？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "The trees on Ox Mountain were once beautiful. But because it borders a great city, axes and hatchets cut them down. Could they remain beautiful? With the respite that day and night provide, and the moisture of rain and dew, buds and sprouts did grow again—but then cattle and sheep came to graze on them. That is why the mountain looks so bare. People see its bareness and suppose it never had timber. But is this the nature of the mountain? And as for what is preserved in a person, how could there be no heart of benevolence and righteousness? The way one lets go of one's good heart is like the axes and hatchets on the trees: hack at it day after day, and can it remain beautiful? With the restorative rest of day and night, and the air of the calm dawn, one's likes and dislikes come close to those of other people—but just barely. Then what one does during the day shackles and destroys it again. When this shackling is repeated over and over, the restorative night air is no longer enough to preserve it. When the night air is no longer enough, one is not far from an animal. Others see one's animality and suppose there was never any good endowment there. But is this truly the nature of a human being? Therefore, given the right nourishment, there is nothing that will not grow; deprived of nourishment, there is nothing that will not wither away. Confucius said: 'Hold on to it and it is preserved; let it go and it is lost. It comes and goes without fixed times, and no one knows its direction.' This was spoken of the heart, was it not?"

passages.text: 孟子曰：「無或乎王之不智也，雖有天下易生之物也，一日暴之、十日寒之，未有能生者也。吾見亦罕矣，吾退而寒之者至矣，吾如有萌焉何哉？今夫弈之為數，小數也；不專心致志，則不得也。弈秋，通國之善弈者也。使弈秋誨二人弈，其一人專心致志，惟弈秋之為聽。一人雖聽之，一心以為有鴻鵠將至，思援弓繳而射之，雖與之俱學，弗若之矣。為是其智弗若與？曰非然也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "Do not be puzzled by the king's lack of wisdom. Even the most easily grown thing in the world—if you expose it to heat for one day and freeze it for ten days, nothing can survive. The occasions on which I see the king are rare, and as soon as I withdraw, those who 'freeze' him arrive. What can I do about any sprouts that may appear? Now take the game of chess—it is a minor art, but without complete concentration and single-minded devotion, you cannot master it. Chess Master Qiu was the best chess player in the country. Suppose he is teaching two students. One concentrates with total devotion, listening only to Chess Master Qiu. The other, though listening, keeps thinking that a swan is about to fly by, and wonders about drawing a bow to shoot it down. Though he studies alongside the first student, he will never be as good. Is this because his intelligence is inferior? I say it is not."

passages.text: 孟子曰：「魚，我所欲也；熊掌，亦我所欲也，二者不可得兼，舍魚而取熊掌者也。生，亦我所欲也；義，亦我所欲也，二者不可得兼，舍生而取義者也。生亦我所欲，所欲有甚於生者，故不為苟得也；死亦我所惡，所惡有甚於死者，故患有所不辟也。如使人之所欲莫甚於生，則凡可以得生者，何不用也？使人之所惡莫甚於死者，則凡可以辟患者，何不為也？由是則生而有不用也，由是則可以辟患而有不為也。是故所欲有甚於生者，所惡有甚於死者，非獨賢者有是心也，人皆有之，賢者能勿喪耳。一簞食，一豆羹，得之則生，弗得則死。嘑爾而與之，行道之人弗受；蹴爾而與之，乞人不屑也。萬鍾則不辨禮義而受之。萬鍾於我何加焉？為宮室之美、妻妾之奉、所識窮乏者得我與？鄉為身死而不受，今為宮室之美為之；鄉為身死而不受，今為妻妾之奉為之；鄉為身死而不受，今為所識窮乏者得我而為之，是亦不可以已乎？此之謂失其本心。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "Fish is something I desire; bear's paw is also something I desire. If I cannot have both, I will give up fish and take bear's paw. Life is something I desire; righteousness is also something I desire. If I cannot have both, I will give up life and take righteousness. Life is indeed something I desire, but there are things I desire more than life, so I will not do anything to get it by improper means. Death is indeed something I detest, but there are things I detest more than death, so there are dangers I will not avoid. If there were nothing people desired more than life, then why would they not use every possible means to survive? If there were nothing people detested more than death, then why would they not do anything to avoid danger? Yet there are means of survival that people will not use, and ways of avoiding danger that people will not take. This shows that there are things people desire more than life, and things they detest more than death. It is not only the worthy who have this heart—all people have it. The worthy are simply those who do not lose it. A single basket of rice, a single bowl of soup—get them and you live, go without and you die. But if they are offered with a contemptuous shout, even a passerby will refuse them. If they are offered with a kick, even a beggar will scorn them. Yet a salary of ten thousand bushels some people accept without regard for propriety and righteousness. What does ten thousand bushels add to me? Is it for the beauty of mansions, the service of wives and concubines, or the gratitude of acquaintances in need? Before, one would have died rather than accept, but now one accepts for the beauty of mansions. Before, one would have died rather than accept, but now one accepts for the service of wives and concubines. Before, one would have died rather than accept, but now one accepts for the gratitude of poor acquaintances. Can this not be stopped? This is called losing one's original heart."

passages.text: 孟子曰：「仁，人心也；義，人路也。舍其路而弗由，放其心而不知求，哀哉！人有雞犬放，則知求之；有放心，而不知求。學問之道無他，求其放心而已矣。」孟子曰：「今有無名之指，屈而不信，非疾痛害事也，如有能信之者，則不遠秦楚之路，為指之不若人也。指不若人，則知惡之；心不若人，則不知惡，此之謂不知類也。」孟子曰：「拱把之桐梓，人苟欲生之，皆知所以養之者。至於身，而不知所以養之者，豈愛身不若桐梓哉？弗思甚也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "Benevolence is the heart of a person; righteousness is the path of a person. To abandon that path and not follow it, to lose that heart and not know to seek it—how sad! When people's chickens and dogs stray, they know to search for them. But when their heart strays, they do not know to search for it. The way of learning is nothing other than seeking the heart that has strayed." Mencius said: "Suppose there is someone whose ring finger is bent and cannot straighten. It is not painful and it does not interfere with his work. Yet if there were someone who could straighten it, he would not consider the road to Qin or Chu too far to travel, because his finger is not as good as other people's. When a finger is not as good as others', one knows to be troubled by it. But when one's heart is not as good as others', one does not know to be troubled. This is called not knowing what matters." Mencius said: "If people have a paulownia or catalpa tree of only a span or two in girth and wish it to grow, they all know how to nourish it. But when it comes to their own selves, they do not know how to nourish themselves. Surely it is not that they care about themselves less than about a paulownia tree? They simply do not think."

passages.text: 孟子曰：「人之於身也，兼所愛。兼所愛，則兼所養也。無尺寸之膚不愛焉，則無尺寸之膚不養也。所以考其善不善者，豈有他哉？於己取之而已矣。體有貴賤，有小大。無以小害大，無以賤害貴。養其小者為小人，養其大者為大人。今有場師，舍其梧檟，養其樲棘，則為賤場師焉。養其一指而失其肩背，而不知也，則為狼疾人也。飲食之人，則人賤之矣，為其養小以失大也。飲食之人無有失也，則口腹豈適為尺寸之膚哉？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "People love every part of their bodies. Since they love every part, they nourish every part. Since there is not an inch of skin they do not love, there is not an inch of skin they do not nourish. To judge whether one nourishes well or poorly, is there any other way than to examine one's own choices? The body has parts of greater and lesser importance, parts that are major and minor. Do not let the minor harm the major; do not let the less important harm the more important. One who nourishes the minor part becomes a petty person; one who nourishes the major part becomes a great person. Consider a gardener who neglects his fine paulownia and catalpa trees but tends his thorns and brambles—he would be a worthless gardener. Someone who takes care of one finger while losing his shoulders and back, without realizing it, is a confused and reckless person. Those who care only about eating and drinking are looked down upon by others, because they nourish the minor at the expense of the major. If a person who cares about eating and drinking lost nothing else thereby, would the mouth and belly be merely an inch of skin?"

passages.text: 公都子問曰：「鈞是人也，或為大人，或為小人，何也？」孟子曰：「從其大體為大人，從其小體為小人。」曰：「鈞是人也，或從其大體，或從其小體，何也？」曰：「耳目之官不思，而蔽於物，物交物，則引之而已矣。心之官則思，思則得之，不思則不得也。此天之所與我者，先立乎其大者，則其小者弗能奪也。此為大人而已矣。」
passages.translation_en: Gongduzi asked: "All are equally human, yet some become great persons and some become petty persons. Why is this?" Mencius said: "Those who follow the greater part of themselves become great persons; those who follow the lesser part become petty persons." "All are equally human, yet some follow the greater part and some follow the lesser. Why?" "The faculties of hearing and sight do not think, and so they are obscured by things. When one thing interacts with another, it simply pulls them along. The faculty of the heart does think. If it thinks, it will find the answer; if it does not think, it will not. This is what Heaven has given us. If one first establishes the greater part of oneself, then the lesser part cannot steal it away. This is simply what makes a great person."

passages.text: 孟子曰：「有天爵者，有人爵者。仁義忠信，樂善不倦，此天爵也；公卿大夫，此人爵也。古之人修其天爵，而人爵從之。今之人修其天爵，以要人爵；既得人爵，而棄其天爵，則惑之甚者也，終亦必亡而已矣。」孟子曰：「欲貴者，人之同心也。人人有貴於己者，弗思耳。人之所貴者，非良貴也。趙孟之所貴，趙孟能賤之。《詩》云：『既醉以酒，既飽以德。』言飽乎仁義也，所以不願人之膏粱之味也；令聞廣譽施於身，所以不願人之文繡也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "There are honors bestowed by Heaven, and honors bestowed by man. Benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, faithfulness, and tireless delight in goodness—these are the honors of Heaven. The ranks of duke, minister, and high official—these are the honors of man. The ancients cultivated their Heavenly honors, and human honors followed naturally. People today cultivate Heavenly honors in order to chase after human honors. Once they get human honors, they discard their Heavenly honors. This is the height of delusion, and in the end they will surely lose everything." Mencius said: "The desire for honor is a feeling shared by all. Yet everyone already has something honorable within themselves—they simply do not reflect on it. The honor that others confer is not true honor. What Zhao Meng ennobles, Zhao Meng can also debase. The Book of Odes says: 'Having been drunk with wine, having been filled with virtue.' This means being filled with benevolence and righteousness, so that one has no craving for the rich flavors of other men's tables; when a fine reputation and broad renown are upon oneself, one has no craving for the embroidered finery of others."

passages.text: 孟子曰：「仁之勝不仁也，猶水勝火。今之為仁者，猶以一杯水，救一車薪之火也；不熄，則謂之水不勝火，此又與於不仁之甚者也。亦終必亡而已矣。」孟子曰：「五穀者，種之美者也；苟為不熟，不如荑稗。夫仁亦在乎熟之而已矣。」孟子曰：「羿之教人射，必志於彀；學者亦必志於彀。大匠誨人，必以規矩；學者亦必以規矩。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: "Benevolence overcomes cruelty the way water overcomes fire. But those who practice benevolence today are like people trying to put out a cartload of burning firewood with a single cup of water. When the fire is not extinguished, they say water cannot overcome fire. This only aids cruelty in the worst way, and in the end they too will surely lose everything." Mencius said: "The five grains are the finest of seeds, but if they do not ripen, they are not as good as wild rice. Benevolence, too, must be brought to full maturity." Mencius said: "When Archer Yi taught people to shoot, he always insisted they draw the bow to its full extent; students must likewise aim for the full draw. When a master carpenter teaches, he always uses the compass and square; students must likewise use the compass and square."

passages.text: 任人有問屋廬子曰：「禮與食孰重？」曰：「禮重。」「色與禮孰重？」曰：「禮重。」曰：「以禮食，則飢而死；不以禮食，則得食，必以禮乎？親迎，則不得妻；不親迎，則得妻，必親迎乎！」
passages.translation_en: A man from Ren asked Wulu Zi: 'Which is more important, ritual propriety or food?' Wulu Zi replied: 'Ritual propriety is more important.' 'Which is more important, sex or ritual propriety?' 'Ritual propriety is more important.' The man pressed: 'If following ritual propriety means starving to death, but ignoring it means getting food, must one still insist on propriety? If performing the formal wedding ceremony means not getting a wife, but skipping it means getting one, must one still insist on the ceremony?'

passages.text: 屋廬子不能對，明日之鄒以告孟子。孟子曰：「於答是也何有？不揣其本而齊其末，方寸之木可使高於岑樓。金重於羽者，豈謂一鉤金與一輿羽之謂哉？取食之重者，與禮之輕者而比之，奚翅食重？取色之重者，與禮之輕者而比之，奚翅色重？往應之曰：『紾兄之臂而奪之食，則得食；不紾，則不得食，則將紾之乎？踰東家牆而摟其處子，則得妻；不摟，則不得妻，則將摟之乎？』」曹交問曰：「人皆可以為堯舜，有諸？」孟子曰：「然。」
passages.translation_en: Wulu Zi could not answer. The next day he went to Zou and told Mencius about it. Mencius said: 'What is so difficult about answering this? If you compare the tops without measuring the bases, you could make an inch-thick piece of wood taller than a towering building. We say gold is heavier than feathers, but does that mean a single clasp of gold outweighs a cartload of feathers? If you take an extreme case of needing food and compare it with a trivial point of ritual, of course food seems more important. If you take an extreme case of sexual desire and compare it with a trivial point of ritual, of course sex seems more important. Go back and tell him this: "If twisting your elder brother's arm would get you food, but not twisting it would leave you hungry, would you twist it? If climbing over your eastern neighbor's wall and seizing their daughter would get you a wife, but not doing so would leave you without one, would you do it?"' Cao Jiao asked: 'People say that anyone can become a Yao or a Shun. Is this true?' Mencius said: 'Yes.'

passages.text: 「交聞文王十尺，湯九尺，今交九尺四寸以長，食粟而已，如何則可？」
passages.translation_en: Cao Jiao said: 'I have heard that King Wen was ten feet tall and Tang was nine feet tall. Now I am over nine feet four inches, yet all I do is eat grain. What must I do to become like them?'

passages.text: 曰：「奚有於是？亦為之而已矣。有人於此，力不能勝一匹雛，則為無力人矣；今曰舉百鈞，則為有力人矣。然則舉烏獲之任，是亦為烏獲而已矣。夫人豈以不勝為患哉？弗為耳。徐行後長者謂之弟，疾行先長者謂之不弟。夫徐行者，豈人所不能哉？所不為也。堯舜之道，孝弟而已矣。子服堯之服，誦堯之言，行堯之行，是堯而已矣；子服桀之服，誦桀之言，行桀之行，是桀而已矣。」曰：「交得見於鄒君，可以假館，願留而受業於門。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'What does height have to do with it? You simply need to act. If someone here cannot lift a single young chicken, he is a man without strength. But if he can lift three thousand catties, then he is a man of great strength. So one who can bear the load of Wu Huo is simply another Wu Huo. Why should anyone worry about being incapable? The problem is simply not trying. Walking slowly behind an elder is called brotherly respect; walking quickly ahead of an elder is called disrespect. Is walking slowly something people cannot do? It is simply something they choose not to do. The Way of Yao and Shun is nothing more than filial piety and brotherly respect. Wear the clothes of Yao, speak the words of Yao, act as Yao acted, and you are simply another Yao. Wear the clothes of Jie, speak the words of Jie, act as Jie acted, and you are simply another Jie.' Cao Jiao said: 'I shall seek an audience with the lord of Zou and ask to stay, so I may study under you.'

passages.text: 曰：「夫道，若大路然，豈難知哉？人病不求耳。子歸而求之，有餘師。」公孫丑問曰：「高子曰：『《小弁》，小人之詩也。』」孟子曰：「何以言之？」曰：「怨。」曰：「固哉，高叟之為《詩》也！有人於此，越人關弓而射之，則己談笑而道之；無他，疏之也。其兄關弓而射之，則己垂涕泣而道之；無他，戚之也。小弁之怨，親親也。親親，仁也。固矣夫，高叟之為《詩》也！」曰：「《凱風》何以不怨？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'The Way is like a broad highway—is it hard to find? People simply fail to seek it. Go home and seek it; you will have teachers enough.' Gongsun Chou said: 'Master Gao says that the "Xiao Bian" ode is the poem of a petty man.' Mencius asked: 'Why does he say that?' 'Because it expresses resentment.' Mencius said: 'How rigid old Master Gao is in his reading of the Odes! Suppose someone here were shot at by a stranger from Yue with a drawn bow—one could talk about it with a laugh, for no other reason than that the attacker is a stranger. But if one's own brother drew a bow and shot, one would speak of it in tears—for no other reason than the closeness of the bond. The resentment of "Xiao Bian" comes from love for one's kin. And love for kin is benevolence itself. How rigid indeed is old Master Gao's reading of the Odes!' Gongsun Chou asked: 'Then why does the "Kai Feng" ode not express resentment?'

passages.text: 曰：「《凱風》，親之過小者也；《小弁》，親之過大者也。親之過大而不怨，是愈疏也；親之過小而怨，是不可磯也。愈疏，不孝也；不可磯，亦不孝也。孔子曰：『舜其至孝矣，五十而慕。』」宋牼將之楚，孟子遇於石丘。曰：「先生將何之？」曰：「吾聞秦楚構兵，我將見楚王說而罷之。楚王不悅，我將見秦王說而罷之，二王我將有所遇焉。」曰：「軻也請無問其詳，願聞其指。說之將何如？」曰：「我將言其不利也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: '"Kai Feng" deals with a minor fault of a parent; "Xiao Bian" deals with a major fault. Not to resent a major fault in a parent is to grow more distant from them. To resent a minor fault is to be overly sensitive. Growing more distant is unfilial; being overly sensitive is also unfilial. Confucius said: "Shun was the most filial of all—at fifty he still yearned for his parents."' Song Keng was on his way to Chu. Mencius met him at Shiqiu and asked: 'Where are you going, sir?' Song Keng replied: 'I have heard that Qin and Chu are waging war. I intend to see the King of Chu and persuade him to stop. If the King of Chu is not receptive, I shall see the King of Qin and persuade him. Of the two kings, I shall find one I can work with.' Mencius said: 'I will not ask for details, but I would like to hear the gist of your approach. How will you persuade them?' Song Keng said: 'I shall explain to them that war is unprofitable.'

passages.text: 曰：「先生之志則大矣，先生之號則不可。先生以利說秦楚之王，秦楚之王悅於利，以罷三軍之師，是三軍之士樂罷而悅於利也。為人臣者懷利以事其君，為人子者懷利以事其父，為人弟者懷利以事其兄。是君臣、父子、兄弟終去仁義，懷利以相接，然而不亡者，未之有也。先生以仁義說秦楚之王，秦楚之王悅於仁義，而罷三軍之師，是三軍之士樂罷而悅於仁義也。為人臣者懷仁義以事其君，為人子者懷仁義以事其父，為人弟者懷仁義以事其兄，是君臣、父子、兄弟去利，懷仁義以相接也。然而不王者，未之有也。何必曰利？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'Your intention is grand, sir, but your banner is wrong. If you persuade the kings of Qin and Chu through profit, and the kings halt their armies because they are pleased by profit, then the soldiers of those three armies will delight in the ceasefire because they too are pleased by profit. Ministers will serve their lords with profit in mind, sons will serve their fathers with profit in mind, younger brothers will serve their elder brothers with profit in mind. Ultimately, rulers and ministers, fathers and sons, brothers—all will abandon benevolence and righteousness, dealing with each other purely through calculations of profit. No state that does this has ever escaped ruin. But if you persuade the kings of Qin and Chu through benevolence and righteousness, and the kings halt their armies because they are pleased by benevolence and righteousness, then the soldiers will delight in the ceasefire because they too are pleased by benevolence and righteousness. Ministers will serve their lords with benevolence and righteousness in mind, sons will serve their fathers so, brothers will serve each other so. Rulers and ministers, fathers and sons, brothers—all will set aside profit and deal with each other through benevolence and righteousness. No one who does this has ever failed to become a true king. Why must you speak of profit?'

passages.text: 孟子居鄒，季任為任處守，以幣交，受之而不報。處於平陸，儲子為相，以幣交，受之而不報。他日由鄒之任，見季子；由平陸之齊，不見儲子。屋廬子喜曰：「連得閒矣。」問曰：「夫子之任見季子，之齊不見儲子，為其為相與？」曰：「非也。《書》曰：『享多儀，儀不及物曰不享，惟不役志于享。』為其不成享也。」屋廬子悅。或問之。屋廬子曰：「季子不得之鄒，儲子得之平陸。」
passages.translation_en: When Mencius was living in Zou, Ji Ren was serving as regent of Ren and sent a gift of silk to establish relations; Mencius accepted it but did not return the visit. When he was in Pinglu, Chu Zi was serving as prime minister of Qi and likewise sent a gift; Mencius accepted it but did not return the visit. Later, when traveling from Zou to Ren, he visited Ji Zi; but when traveling from Pinglu to Qi, he did not visit Chu Zi. Wulu Zi was pleased and said: 'I have found an opening to ask about this.' He asked: 'Master, when you went to Ren you visited Ji Zi, but when you went to Qi you did not visit Chu Zi. Was it because Chu Zi was merely a prime minister?' Mencius said: 'No. The Book of Documents says: "A gift offering requires proper ceremony; if the ceremony does not match the gift, it is as if no gift were offered—for the will must not be enslaved by the offering." It was because his offering did not constitute a proper gift.' Wulu Zi was satisfied. When someone asked him about it, Wulu Zi explained: 'Ji Zi could not come to Zou himself, but Chu Zi could have come to Pinglu.'

passages.text: 淳于髡曰：「先名實者，為人也；後名實者，自為也。夫子在三卿之中，名實未加於上下而去之，仁者固如此乎？」孟子曰：「居下位，不以賢事不肖者，伯夷也；五就湯，五就桀者，伊尹也；不惡汙君，不辭小官者，柳下惠也。三子者不同道，其趨一也。一者何也？曰：仁也。君子亦仁而已矣，何必同？」
passages.translation_en: Chunyu Kun said: 'Those who put reputation and substance first are acting for others; those who put them last are acting for themselves. You, Master, were ranked among the three senior ministers, yet before your reputation and achievements could benefit either the ruler above or the people below, you left. Is this really how a benevolent man behaves?' Mencius replied: 'One who holds a low position and refuses to serve an unworthy lord with his talents—that was Bo Yi. One who went to Tang five times and to Jie five times—that was Yi Yin. One who did not disdain a corrupt lord or decline a petty office—that was Liuxia Hui. These three men followed different paths, but their destination was the same. And what was that? Benevolence. A gentleman need only be benevolent. Why must everyone follow the same path?'

passages.text: 曰：「魯繆公之時，公儀子為政，子柳、子思為臣，魯之削也滋甚。若是乎賢者之無益於國也！」曰：「虞不用百里奚而亡，秦穆公用之而霸。不用賢則亡，削何可得與？」曰：「昔者王豹處於淇，而河西善謳；緜駒處於高唐，而齊右善歌；華周、杞梁之妻善哭其夫，而變國俗。有諸內必形諸外。為其事而無其功者，髡未嘗覩之也。是故無賢者也，有則髡必識之。」
passages.translation_en: Chunyu Kun said: 'In the time of Duke Mu of Lu, Gongyi Zi managed the government, and Zi Liu and Zi Si served as ministers, yet Lu's territory was carved away worse than ever. This shows that worthy men are of no benefit to a state!' Mencius replied: 'The state of Yu did not employ Baili Xi and perished; Duke Mu of Qin employed him and became hegemon. Failing to employ the worthy leads to ruin—mere territorial loss would be getting off lightly.' Chunyu Kun continued: 'In the past, when Wang Bao lived by the Qi River, the people west of the Yellow River became excellent singers. When Mian Ju lived in Gaotang, the people in the right part of Qi became excellent singers. When the wives of Hua Zhou and Qi Liang mourned their husbands with such skill, they transformed the customs of the entire state. What is within must manifest without. I have never seen anyone perform the work without achieving results. Therefore there are no worthy men today—if there were, I would certainly recognize them.'

passages.text: 曰：「孔子為魯司寇，不用，從而祭，燔肉不至，不稅冕而行。不知者以為為肉也。其知者以為為無禮也。乃孔子則欲以微罪行，不欲為苟去。君子之所為，眾人固不識也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'When Confucius served as Minister of Justice in Lu and his counsel was not followed, he attended a sacrifice and when the ceremonial meat was not sent to him as was proper, he left without even removing his ceremonial cap. Those who did not understand him thought it was over the meat. Those who understood him knew it was over the breach of propriety. As for Confucius himself, he wished to leave over a minor offense rather than depart without any cause at all. The actions of a gentleman are naturally beyond the understanding of ordinary people.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「五霸者，三王之罪人也；今之諸侯，五霸之罪人也；今之大夫，今之諸侯之罪人也。天子適諸侯曰巡狩，諸侯朝於天子曰述職。春省耕而補不足，秋省斂而助不給。入其疆，土地辟，田野治，養老尊賢，俊傑在位，則有慶，慶以地。入其疆，土地荒蕪，遺老失賢，掊克在位，則有讓。一不朝，則貶其爵；再不朝，則削其地；三不朝，則六師移之。是故天子討而不伐，諸侯伐而不討。五霸者，摟諸侯以伐諸侯者也，故曰：五霸者，三王之罪人也。
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'The Five Hegemons were sinners against the Three Kings. The feudal lords of today are sinners against the Five Hegemons. The ministers of today are sinners against their own feudal lords. When the Son of Heaven visited the feudal lords, it was called an inspection tour. When the feudal lords came to the Son of Heaven, it was called reporting on their duties. In spring, the inspection checked the plowing and made up for any shortages; in autumn, it checked the harvest and aided where supplies were lacking. When one entered a state and found the land opened up, the fields well managed, the elderly cared for, the worthy honored, and outstanding men in office, there would be rewards—rewards of additional territory. When one entered a state and found the land overgrown, the elderly neglected, the worthy ignored, and extortioners in office, there would be reprimand. If a lord failed to attend court once, his rank was reduced. If he failed twice, his territory was cut. If he failed three times, the six armies were sent to remove him. Thus the Son of Heaven would censure but not personally attack; the feudal lords would attack but not censure. The Five Hegemons, however, coerced the feudal lords to attack other feudal lords. That is why I say the Five Hegemons were sinners against the Three Kings.'

passages.text: 「五霸，桓公為盛。葵丘之會諸侯，束牲、載書而不歃血。初命曰：『誅不孝，無易樹子，無以妾為妻。』再命曰：『尊賢育才，以彰有德。』三命曰：『敬老慈幼，無忘賓旅。』四命曰：『士無世官，官事無攝，取士必得，無專殺大夫。』五命曰：『無曲防，無遏糴，無有封而不告。』曰：『凡我同盟之人，既盟之後，言歸于好。』今之諸侯，皆犯此五禁，故曰：今之諸侯，五霸之罪人也。
passages.translation_en: 'Of the Five Hegemons, Duke Huan of Qi was the greatest. At the covenant at Kuiqiu, the feudal lords bound the sacrificial animals and placed the written covenant on them, but did not smear their lips with blood. The first injunction said: "Punish the unfilial; do not set aside the designated heir; do not elevate a concubine to the status of wife." The second said: "Honor the worthy and nurture the talented, so as to distinguish the virtuous." The third said: "Respect the elderly and care for the young; do not neglect travelers and guests." The fourth said: "Officials shall not hold hereditary office; one office shall not be given multiple duties; selection of officials must be based on merit; do not execute ministers arbitrarily." The fifth said: "Do not build crooked dikes; do not block grain trade; do not grant fiefs without reporting them." It was declared: "All of us who have joined this covenant shall return to amicable relations after pledging." The feudal lords of today all violate these five prohibitions. That is why I say the feudal lords of today are sinners against the Five Hegemons.'

passages.text: 「長君之惡其罪小，逢君之惡其罪大。今之大夫，皆逢君之惡，故曰：今之大夫，今之諸侯之罪人也。」魯欲使慎子為將軍。孟子曰：「不教民而用之，謂之殃民。殃民者，不容於堯舜之世。一戰勝齊，遂有南陽，然且不可。」慎子勃然不悅曰：「此則滑釐所不識也。」
passages.translation_en: 'To indulge a ruler's faults is a small crime; to actively encourage a ruler's faults is a great crime. The ministers of today all encourage their lords' faults. That is why I say the ministers of today are sinners against their own feudal lords.' The state of Lu wanted to appoint Shen Zi as commander of the army. Mencius said: 'To send the people to war without first training them is to bring disaster upon them. One who brings disaster upon the people would not have been tolerated in the age of Yao and Shun. Even if you could defeat Qi in a single battle and take Nanyang, it still should not be done.' Shen Zi was displeased and said: 'This is something I, Hua Li, cannot understand.'

passages.text: 曰：「吾明告子。天子之地方千里；不千里，不足以待諸侯。諸侯之地方百里；不百里，不足以守宗廟之典籍。周公之封於魯，為方百里也；地非不足，而儉於百里。太公之封於齊也，亦為方百里也；地非不足也，而儉於百里。今魯方百里者五，子以為有王者作，則魯在所損乎？在所益乎？徒取諸彼以與此，然且仁者不為，況於殺人以求之乎？君子之事君也，務引其君以當道，志於仁而已。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'Let me explain it plainly. The territory of the Son of Heaven is a thousand li square; without a thousand li, it would not be enough to receive the feudal lords. The territory of a feudal lord is a hundred li square; without a hundred li, it would not be enough to maintain the ancestral temples and their records. When the Duke of Zhou was enfeoffed in Lu, his territory was a hundred li square. The land was not insufficient, yet it was kept to only a hundred li. When Taigong was enfeoffed in Qi, his territory was also a hundred li square. The land was not insufficient, yet it was kept to only a hundred li. Now Lu has five times a hundred li. Do you think that if a true king arose, Lu would gain territory or lose it? Even taking from others to give to the deserving, a benevolent man would not do—how much less would he do so by killing people to get it? The way a gentleman serves his ruler is to guide him onto the proper path and set his will on benevolence, nothing more.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「今之事君者曰：『我能為君辟土地，充府庫。』今之所謂良臣，古之所謂民賊也。君不鄉道，不志於仁，而求富之，是富桀也。『我能為君約與國，戰必克。』今之所謂良臣，古之所謂民賊也。君不鄉道，不志於仁，而求為之強戰，是輔桀也。由今之道，無變今之俗，雖與之天下，不能一朝居也。」白圭曰：「吾欲二十而取一，何如？」孟子曰：「子之道，貉道也。萬室之國，一人陶，則可乎？」曰：「不可，器不足用也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'Ministers who serve their lords today say: "I can expand territory for my lord and fill his treasury." What today is called a good minister would in ancient times be called a robber of the people. If a ruler does not incline toward the Way or set his will on benevolence, to seek to enrich him is to enrich a tyrant like Jie. Others say: "I can forge alliances and win every battle for my lord." What today is called a good minister would in ancient times be called a robber of the people. If a ruler does not incline toward the Way or set his will on benevolence, to seek to strengthen his military is to aid a tyrant like Jie. Following today's path without changing today's customs, even if you gave such a ruler the whole world, he could not hold it for a single morning.' Bai Gui said: 'I would like to tax at one part in twenty. What do you think?' Mencius said: 'Your way is the way of the northern barbarians. In a city of ten thousand households, would it suffice to have a single potter?' Bai Gui said: 'No—there would not be enough wares.'

passages.text: 曰：「夫貉，五穀不生，惟黍生之。無城郭、宮室、宗廟、祭祀之禮，無諸侯幣帛饔飧，無百官有司，故二十取一而足也。今居中國，去人倫，無君子，如之何其可也？陶以寡，且不可以為國，況無君子乎？欲輕之於堯舜之道者，大貉小貉也；欲重之於堯舜之道者，大桀小桀也。」白圭曰：「丹之治水也愈於禹。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'In the northern barbarian lands, the five grains do not grow; only millet grows there. They have no city walls, no palaces, no ancestral temples, no ritual sacrifices, no diplomatic gift exchanges, no bureaucracy of officials. Therefore taxing at one in twenty is enough for them. But now, living in the Central Kingdom, to abolish human relationships and do away with gentlemen—how could that be acceptable? With too few potters, you cannot sustain a state; how much less can you sustain one without gentlemen? Those who wish to make taxes lighter than the Way of Yao and Shun are, to a greater or lesser degree, barbarians. Those who wish to make them heavier than the Way of Yao and Shun are, to a greater or lesser degree, tyrants like Jie.' Bai Gui said: 'My management of floods is superior to Yu's.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「子過矣。禹之治水，水之道也。是故禹以四海為壑，今吾子以鄰國為壑。水逆行，謂之洚水。洚水者，洪水也，仁人之所惡也。吾子過矣。」孟子曰：「君子不亮，惡乎執？」魯欲使樂正子為政。孟子曰：「吾聞之，喜而不寐。」公孫丑曰：「樂正子強乎？」曰：「否。」「有知慮乎？」曰：「否。」「多聞識乎？」曰：「否。」「然則奚為喜而不寐？」曰：「其為人也好善。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'You are wrong, sir. When Yu controlled the floods, he worked with the natural course of water. That is why Yu used the four seas as his drainage basin. But you, sir, use the neighboring states as your drainage basin. When water flows backward, it is called a deluge. A deluge is a flood—something a benevolent person detests. You are wrong, sir.' Mencius also said: 'If a gentleman is not sincere, how can he hold firm to anything?' The state of Lu wanted to appoint Yue Zheng Zi to manage the government. Mencius said: 'When I heard this, I was so happy I could not sleep.' Gongsun Chou asked: 'Is Yue Zheng Zi a man of vigor?' Mencius said: 'No.' 'Is he a man of wisdom and foresight?' 'No.' 'Is he a man of wide learning?' 'No.' 'Then why were you so happy you could not sleep?' Mencius said: 'Because he is a man who loves goodness.'

passages.text: 「好善足乎？」曰：「好善優於天下，而況魯國乎？夫苟好善，則四海之內，皆將輕千里而來告之以善。夫苟不好善，則人將曰：『訑訑，予既已知之矣。』訑訑之聲音顏色，距人於千里之外。士止於千里之外，則讒諂面諛之人至矣。與讒諂面諛之人居，國欲治，可得乎？」陳子曰：「古之君子何如則仕？」
passages.translation_en: 'Is loving goodness enough?' Mencius said: 'Loving goodness is more than enough to govern the whole world, let alone the state of Lu. If a person truly loves goodness, then people from within the four seas will think nothing of traveling a thousand li to come and tell him of what is good. But if he does not love goodness, people will say: "How smug he is—he already thinks he knows everything." That smug tone and expression will keep people a thousand li away. When worthy men stay a thousand li away, then slanderers, flatterers, and sycophants will arrive. And if one surrounds oneself with slanderers, flatterers, and sycophants, can one hope to govern the state well?' Chen Zi asked: 'Under what conditions did the gentlemen of antiquity take office?'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「所就三，所去三。迎之致敬以有禮，言將行其言也，則就之；禮貌未衰，言弗行也，則去之。其次，雖未行其言也，迎之致敬以有禮，則就之；禮貌衰，則去之。其下，朝不食，夕不食，飢餓不能出門戶。君聞之曰：『吾大者不能行其道，又不能從其言也，使飢餓於我土地，吾恥之。』周之，亦可受也，免死而已矣。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'There were three conditions for accepting office and three for leaving. First: if the ruler welcomes you with respect and due ceremony, indicating he intends to follow your counsel—then accept. If courtesies remain but your counsel goes unfollowed—then leave. Second: even if your counsel is not yet followed, if the ruler still welcomes you with respect and due ceremony—then accept. If courtesies decline—then leave. Third: if you have had neither breakfast nor supper and are so hungry you cannot leave your door, and the ruler learns of it and says, "I am ashamed that I cannot follow his Way or even heed his words, yet I let him starve in my domain"—then you may accept his relief. But only to escape death, nothing more.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「舜發於畎畝之中，傅說舉於版築之閒，膠鬲舉於魚鹽之中，管夷吾舉於士，孫叔敖舉於海，百里奚舉於市。故天將降大任於是人也，必先苦其心志，勞其筋骨，餓其體膚，空乏其身，行拂亂其所為，所以動心忍性，曾益其所不能。人恒過，然後能改；困於心，衡於慮，而後作；徵於色，發於聲，而後喻。入則無法家拂士，出則無敵國外患者，國恒亡。然後知生於憂患而死於安樂也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'Shun rose from the fields; Fu Yue was raised from among the builders; Jiao Ge was raised from among the fish and salt traders; Guan Zhong was raised from the hands of his jailer; Sun Shu Ao was raised from the seacoast; Baili Xi was raised from the marketplace. Thus, when Heaven is about to confer a great responsibility on a person, it first makes his heart and will suffer, exhausts his muscles and bones, starves his body, subjects him to poverty, and confounds his every endeavor—all so as to stir his heart, toughen his nature, and develop abilities he did not have before. People constantly make mistakes, and only then can they correct themselves. They are troubled in mind and burdened in thought, and only then do they act. Their feelings show on their faces and come out in their voices, and only then are they understood. A state that has no families of law-abiding tradition and no ministers who can remonstrate within, and no rival states or external threats without, will invariably perish. From this we understand that life springs from adversity, and death comes from ease and comfort.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「教亦多術矣，予不屑之教誨也者，是亦教誨之而已矣。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'There are many methods of teaching. When I deem someone unworthy of my instruction, that in itself is a form of instruction.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「盡其心者，知其性也。知其性，則知天矣。存其心，養其性，所以事天也。殀壽不貳，修身以俟之，所以立命也。」孟子曰：「莫非命也，順受其正。是故知命者，不立乎巖牆之下。盡其道而死者，正命也。桎梏死者，非正命也。」孟子曰：「求則得之，舍則失之，是求有益於得也，求在我者也。求之有道，得之有命，是求無益於得也，求在外者也。」孟子曰：「萬物皆備於我矣。反身而誠，樂莫大焉。強恕而行，求仁莫近焉。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'To fully develop one's mind is to understand one's nature. To understand one's nature is to understand Heaven. To preserve one's mind and nourish one's nature — this is how one serves Heaven. Whether one dies young or lives long, one does not waver, but cultivates oneself and awaits what comes — this is how one establishes one's destiny.' Mencius said: 'Everything is destiny — accept it and follow what is proper. Therefore, one who understands destiny does not stand beneath a crumbling wall. To die having fully walked one's path — that is a proper destiny. To die in chains and shackles — that is not a proper destiny.' Mencius said: 'Seek it and you will find it; let it go and you will lose it — this is seeking that benefits the finding, for what is sought lies within oneself. There is a proper way to seek, yet obtaining depends on destiny — this is seeking that does not benefit the finding, for what is sought lies outside oneself.' Mencius said: 'All things are complete within me. To turn inward and find sincerity — there is no greater joy than this. To practice empathy with vigor — there is no closer path to benevolence than this.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「行之而不著焉，習矣而不察焉，終身由之而不知其道者，眾也。」孟子曰：「人不可以無恥。無恥之恥，無恥矣。」孟子曰：「恥之於人大矣。為機變之巧者，無所用恥焉。不恥不若人，何若人有？」孟子曰：「古之賢王好善而忘勢，古之賢士何獨不然？樂其道而忘人之勢。故王公不致敬盡禮，則不得亟見之。見且猶不得亟，而況得而臣之乎？」孟子謂宋句踐曰：「子好遊乎？吾語子遊。人知之，亦囂囂；人不知，亦囂囂。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'To act without understanding why, to practice without examining what one does, to follow a path all one's life without knowing where it leads — such is the common person.' Mencius said: 'A person must not be without a sense of shame. The shame of having no shame — that itself is true shamelessness.' Mencius said: 'The sense of shame is of great importance to a person. Those who are clever at scheming and deception have no use for shame. If one feels no shame at being inferior to others, how will one ever become their equal?' Mencius said: 'The worthy kings of old loved goodness and forgot about their power. Were the worthy scholars of old any different? They delighted in the Way and forgot about the power of others. Therefore, if kings and dukes did not show the utmost respect and full propriety, they could not see such scholars frequently. If they could not even see them frequently, how much less could they make them serve as ministers!' Mencius said to Song Goujian: 'Do you enjoy traveling to seek office? Let me tell you about such traveling. If others recognize you, be content and at ease; if others do not recognize you, be equally content and at ease.'

passages.text: 曰：「何如斯可以囂囂矣？」曰：「尊德樂義，則可以囂囂矣。故士窮不失義，達不離道。窮不失義，故士得己焉；達不離道，故民不失望焉。古之人，得志，澤加於民；不得志，脩身見於世。窮則獨善其身，達則兼善天下。」孟子曰：「待文王而後興者，凡民也。若夫豪傑之士，雖無文王猶興。」孟子曰：「附之以韓魏之家，如其自視欿然，則過人遠矣。」孟子曰：「以佚道使民，雖勞不怨；以生道殺民，雖死不怨殺者。」
passages.translation_en: Song Goujian asked: 'How can one be so content and at ease?' Mencius replied: 'If you honor virtue and delight in righteousness, then you can be content and at ease. Therefore, when a scholar is in poverty, he does not abandon righteousness; when he succeeds, he does not depart from the Way. In poverty he does not abandon righteousness, and so he retains his self-respect; in success he does not depart from the Way, and so the people are not disappointed. The ancients, when they achieved their aims, spread their blessings to the people; when they did not achieve their aims, they cultivated themselves and made their virtue visible to the world. In poverty, they perfected their own character; in success, they perfected the whole world.' Mencius said: 'Those who waited for King Wen before they were stirred to action were ordinary people. As for the truly outstanding — they would rise even without a King Wen.' Mencius said: 'If you added to someone the wealth of the great houses of Han and Wei, and they still regarded themselves as lacking, then they would surpass others by far.' Mencius said: 'If you employ the people in a way that gives them ease, they will not complain even when they toil. If you take life in a way that gives life, the people will not blame you even when they die.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「霸者之民，驩虞如也；王者之民，皞皞如也。殺之而不怨，利之而不庸，民日遷善而不知為之者。夫君子所過者化，所存者神，上下與天地同流，豈曰小補之哉？」孟子曰：「仁言，不如仁聲之入人深也。善政，不如善教之得民也。善政民畏之，善教民愛之；善政得民財，善教得民心。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'The people under a hegemon are pleased and cheerful; the people under a true king are expansive and at ease. He may execute them, yet they do not resent him; he may benefit them, yet they do not feel the need to give thanks. Day by day the people move toward goodness without knowing who brings it about. Wherever the noble person passes, transformation follows; wherever he dwells, the effect is spiritual. Above and below, he flows together with Heaven and Earth — how can this be called a small contribution?' Mencius said: 'Benevolent words do not penetrate as deeply into people as the reputation of benevolence. Good governance does not win the people as effectively as good education. The people fear good governance; the people love good education. Good governance wins the people's wealth; good education wins the people's hearts.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「人之所不學而能者，其良能也；所不慮而知者，其良知也。孩提之童，無不知愛其親者；及其長也，無不知敬其兄也。親親，仁也；敬長，義也。無他，達之天下也。」孟子曰：「舜之居深山之中，與木石居，與鹿豕遊，其所以異於深山之野人者幾希。及其聞一善言，見一善行，若決江河，沛然莫之能禦也。」孟子曰：「無為其所不為，無欲其所不欲，如此而已矣。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'What a person can do without having learned it — that is innate ability. What a person knows without having to think about it — that is innate knowledge. Every small child knows to love its parents; as children grow older, they all know to respect their elder brothers. Loving one's parents is benevolence; respecting one's elders is righteousness. There is nothing else to it — these simply extend to all under Heaven.' Mencius said: 'When Shun dwelt deep in the mountains, living among trees and rocks, roaming with deer and wild boars, he differed very little from the wild men of the deep mountains. But when he heard a single good word or saw a single good deed, it was like a river bursting through its banks — a mighty flood that nothing could hold back.' Mencius said: 'Do not do what you would not do; do not desire what you would not desire. That is all there is to it.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「人之有德慧術知者，恒存乎疢疾。獨孤臣孽子，其操心也危，其慮患也深，故達。」孟子曰：「有事君人者，事是君則為容悅者也。有安社稷臣者，以安社稷為悅者也。有天民者，達可行於天下而後行之者也。有大人者，正己而物正者也。」孟子曰：「君子有三樂，而王天下不與存焉。父母俱存，兄弟無故，一樂也。仰不愧於天，俯不怍於人，二樂也。得天下英才而教育之，三樂也。君子有三樂，而王天下不與存焉。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'Those who possess moral insight, wisdom, skill, and knowledge usually have endured hardship and affliction. It is the lonely minister and the son born of a concubine — their hearts are beset with anxiety and their thoughts run deep in contemplating danger — and therefore they achieve understanding.' Mencius said: 'There are those who serve their lord merely to please and ingratiate themselves. There are ministers of the altars of state, who find their joy in securing the state. There are those born to serve Heaven, who act only when their principles can be carried out throughout the world. And there are great persons who rectify themselves and all things are rectified along with them.' Mencius said: 'The noble person has three joys, and being king of the world is not among them. That both parents are alive and brothers are without trouble — this is the first joy. That looking up one is not ashamed before Heaven, and looking down one is not ashamed before other people — this is the second joy. To obtain the outstanding talents of the world and educate them — this is the third joy. The noble person has three joys, and being king of the world is not among them.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「廣土眾民，君子欲之，所樂不存焉。中天下而立，定四海之民，君子樂之，所性不存焉。君子所性，雖大行不加焉，雖窮居不損焉，分定故也。君子所性，仁義禮智根於心。其生色也，睟然見於面，盎於背，施於四體，四體不言而喻。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'Vast territory and a large population — the noble person desires these, but his joy does not lie in them. To stand at the center of the world and bring peace to the people within the four seas — the noble person delights in this, but his essential nature does not lie in it. What constitutes the noble person's essential nature is not increased by great accomplishments nor diminished by straitened circumstances, for it is a settled endowment. The noble person's essential nature is benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, rooted in the heart. Their outward manifestation is a pure radiance seen in the face, fullness across the back, and expression throughout the four limbs — the four limbs communicate it without words.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「伯夷辟紂，居北海之濱，聞文王作興，曰：『盍歸乎來！吾聞西伯善養老者。』太公辟紂，居東海之濱，聞文王作興，曰：『盍歸乎來！吾聞西伯善養老者。』天下有善養老，則仁人以為己歸矣。五畝之宅，樹牆下以桑，匹婦蠶之，則老者足以衣帛矣。五母雞，二母彘，無失其時，老者足以無失肉矣。百畝之田，匹夫耕之，八口之家足以無飢矣。所謂西伯善養老者，制其田里，教之樹畜，導其妻子，使養其老。五十非帛不煖，七十非肉不飽。不煖不飽，謂之凍餒。文王之民，無凍餒之老者，此之謂也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'Bo Yi fled from the tyrant Zhou and settled on the shore of the North Sea. When he heard that King Wen had arisen, he said: "Why not go home! I have heard that the Lord of the West takes good care of the elderly." Taigong fled from the tyrant Zhou and settled on the shore of the East Sea. When he heard that King Wen had arisen, he said: "Why not go home! I have heard that the Lord of the West takes good care of the elderly." When there is someone in the world who takes good care of the elderly, benevolent people will look to him as their refuge. With a homestead of five mu, plant mulberry trees along the walls. If the wife tends silkworms, the elderly will have enough to wear silk. With five hens and two sows, if their breeding seasons are not missed, the elderly will have enough to eat meat. With a hundred mu of farmland, if one man tills it, a family of eight will not go hungry. When we say the Lord of the West took good care of the elderly, it means he regulated their fields and homesteads, taught them to plant and raise livestock, and guided their wives and children to care for the aged. At fifty, one cannot stay warm without silk; at seventy, one cannot be satisfied without meat. To be neither warm nor full is called suffering cold and hunger. Among King Wen's people, there were no elderly who suffered cold and hunger — this is what the saying means.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「易其田疇，薄其稅斂，民可使富也。食之以時，用之以禮，財不可勝用也。民非水火不生活，昏暮叩人之門戶，求水火，無弗與者，至足矣。聖人治天下，使有菽粟如水火。菽粟如水火，而民焉有不仁者乎？」孟子曰：「孔子登東山而小魯，登太山而小天下。故觀於海者難為水，遊於聖人之門者難為言。觀水有術，必觀其瀾。日月有明，容光必照焉。流水之為物也，不盈科不行；君子之志於道也，不成章不達。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'Make their fields easy to work, lighten their taxes, and the people can be made wealthy. If they consume in due season and spend according to propriety, wealth will be more than sufficient. People cannot live without water and fire. Knock on someone's door at dusk asking for water or fire, and no one will refuse — because these are so abundant. If a sage governed the world, he would make grain and millet as abundant as water and fire. If grain and millet were as abundant as water and fire, how could the people fail to be benevolent?' Mencius said: 'Confucius climbed East Mountain and Lu seemed small; he climbed Mount Tai and the whole world seemed small. Therefore, one who has gazed upon the sea finds it hard to think of anything else as water; one who has studied at the gate of a sage finds it hard to think of anything else as worthy discourse. In observing water, there is a method — one must observe its waves. The sun and moon possess brightness, and their light inevitably illuminates every crevice. The nature of flowing water is that it does not advance until it has filled each hollow. The noble person who sets his will upon the Way does not achieve mastery until he has completed each stage.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「雞鳴而起，孳孳為善者，舜之徒也。雞鳴而起，孳孳為利者，蹠之徒也。欲知舜與蹠之分，無他，利與善之閒也。」孟子曰：「楊子取為我，拔一毛而利天下，不為也。墨子兼愛，摩頂放踵利天下，為之。子莫執中，執中為近之，執中無權，猶執一也。所惡執一者，為其賊道也，舉一而廢百也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'He who rises at cockcrow and devotes himself tirelessly to goodness is a follower of Shun. He who rises at cockcrow and devotes himself tirelessly to profit is a follower of the robber Zhi. If you wish to know the difference between Shun and Zhi, it is nothing else — it is the space between profit and goodness.' Mencius said: 'Yang Zhu chose "for myself" — even if pulling out a single hair would have benefited the whole world, he would not do it. Mozi embraced universal love — even if it wore him from head to heel for the benefit of the world, he would do it. Zi Mo held to the middle. Holding to the middle comes closer to being right, but holding to the middle without flexibility is the same as holding to one extreme. What is wrong with clinging to one extreme is that it damages the Way — seizing on one thing while neglecting a hundred others.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「飢者甘食，渴者甘飲，是未得飲食之正也，飢渴害之也。豈惟口腹有飢渴之害？人心亦皆有害。人能無以飢渴之害為心害，則不及人不為憂矣。」孟子曰：「柳下惠不以三公易其介。」孟子曰：「有為者辟若掘井，掘井九軔而不及泉，猶為棄井也。」孟子曰：「堯舜，性之也；湯武，身之也；五霸，假之也。久假而不歸，惡知其非有也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'The hungry find any food sweet; the thirsty find any drink delicious. This is not experiencing the true taste of food and drink — hunger and thirst have distorted it. Is it only the mouth and belly that suffer the distortion of hunger and thirst? The human heart-mind is equally subject to such distortion. If a person can avoid letting the damage of hunger and thirst become damage to the heart-mind, then failing to measure up to others will be no cause for worry.' Mencius said: 'Liuxia Hui would not have exchanged his integrity for the rank of one of the Three Dukes.' Mencius said: 'One who undertakes something is like one digging a well. You may dig down nine fathoms, but if you have not yet reached water, it is still an abandoned well.' Mencius said: 'Yao and Shun possessed benevolence by nature; Tang and Wu embodied it through personal effort; the Five Hegemons merely borrowed it. But if one borrows something long enough without returning it, how can one be sure it is not truly one's own?'

passages.text: 公孫丑曰：「伊尹曰：『予不狎于不順。』放太甲于桐，民大悅。太甲賢。又反之，民大悅。賢者之為人臣也，其君不賢，則固可放與？」孟子曰：「有伊尹之志，則可；無伊尹之志，則篡也。」公孫丑曰：「《詩》曰：『不素餐兮』，君子之不耕而食，何也？」孟子曰：「君子居是國也，其君用之，則安富尊榮；其子弟從之，則孝弟忠信。『不素餐兮』，孰大於是？」王子墊問曰：「士何事？」孟子曰：「尚志。」曰：「何謂尚志？」
passages.translation_en: Gongsun Chou said: 'Yi Yin said: "I will not be familiar with what is not right." He banished Tai Jia to Tong, and the people were greatly pleased. When Tai Jia became virtuous, Yi Yin restored him, and the people were again greatly pleased. When a worthy person serves as minister and his ruler is not virtuous, may he indeed banish him?' Mencius said: 'If he has Yi Yin's purpose, then he may. Without Yi Yin's purpose, it would be usurpation.' Gongsun Chou said: 'The Book of Odes says: "He does not eat the bread of idleness." Why is it that the noble person does not farm yet still eats?' Mencius said: 'When a noble person resides in a state and that ruler employs him, there is peace, prosperity, honor, and glory. When the young people follow him, they become filial, respectful, loyal, and trustworthy. "Not eating the bread of idleness" — what could be greater than this?' Prince Dian asked: 'What is the task of the scholar?' Mencius said: 'To elevate his aspirations.' 'What does that mean — to elevate his aspirations?'

passages.text: 曰：「仁義而已矣。殺一無罪，非仁也；非其有而取之，非義也。居惡在？仁是也；路惡在？義是也。居仁由義，大人之事備矣。」孟子曰：「仲子，不義與之齊國而弗受，人皆信之，是舍簞食豆羹之義也。人莫大焉亡親戚、君臣、上下。以其小者信其大者，奚可哉？」桃應問曰：「舜為天子，皋陶為士，瞽瞍殺人，則如之何？」孟子曰：「執之而已矣。」「然則舜不禁與？」曰：「夫舜惡得而禁之？夫有所受之也。」「然則舜如之何？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'Benevolence and righteousness — that is all. To kill a single innocent person is not benevolent; to take what is not one's own is not righteous. Where should one dwell? In benevolence. What road should one travel? Righteousness. To dwell in benevolence and walk the path of righteousness — this is the full task of a great person.' Mencius said: 'Chen Zhongzi refused to accept the state of Qi when it was offered to him unjustly, and everyone believed in his integrity. But this is the kind of righteousness that applies only to a basket of rice or a bowl of soup. No transgression is greater than abandoning the obligations of kinship, ruler and minister, superior and subordinate. To take someone's reliability in small matters as proof of their reliability in great matters — how can that be acceptable?' Tao Ying asked: 'If Shun were the Son of Heaven and Gao Yao were the judge, and Shun's father Gu Sou killed a man, what would happen?' Mencius said: 'Gao Yao would simply arrest him.' 'Would Shun not forbid it?' Mencius said: 'How could Shun forbid it? Gao Yao had received his authority from the law.'  'Then what would Shun do?'

passages.text: 曰：「舜視棄天下，猶棄敝蹝也。竊負而逃，遵海濱而處，終身訢然，樂而忘天下。」孟子自范之齊，望見齊王之子。喟然歎曰：「居移氣，養移體，大哉居乎！夫非盡人之子與？」孟子曰：「王子宮室、車馬、衣服多與人同，而王子若彼者，其居使之然也；況居天下之廣居者乎？魯君之宋，呼於垤澤之門。守者曰：『此非吾君也，何其聲之似我君也？』此無他，居相似也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'Shun would have regarded abandoning the empire as no more than discarding a worn-out sandal. He would have secretly carried his father on his back and fled, settled along the seashore, and lived out his days in happiness, content and forgetful of the empire.' When Mencius traveled from Fan to Qi, he caught sight of the King of Qi's son from a distance. With a deep sigh he said: 'One's surroundings transform one's spirit, and one's nourishment transforms one's body. How great is the influence of one's surroundings! Are we not all equally the children of other people?' Mencius said: 'The prince's residence, carriages and horses, and clothing are largely the same as other people's. That the prince appears as he does is because his surroundings have made him so. How much more so for one who dwells in the vast abode of the whole world! When the Lord of Lu visited Song, he called out at the gate of Die Marsh. The gatekeeper said: "This is not my lord — why does his voice sound so much like my lord's?" This was for no other reason than that their surroundings were similar.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「食而弗愛，豕交之也；愛而不敬，獸畜之也。恭敬者，幣之未將者也。恭敬而無實，君子不可虛拘。」孟子曰：「形色，天性也；惟聖人，然後可以踐形。」齊宣王欲短喪。公孫丑曰：「為朞之喪，猶愈於已乎？」孟子曰：「是猶或紾其兄之臂，子謂之姑徐徐云爾，亦教之孝弟而已矣。」王子有其母死者，其傅為之請數月之喪。公孫丑曰：「若此者，何如也？」曰：「是欲終之而不可得也。雖加一日愈於已，謂夫莫之禁而弗為者也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'To feed someone without showing love is to treat them like a pig. To love someone without showing respect is to keep them like a household animal. Respect and reverence come before any gifts are presented. If there is respect without substance behind it, the noble person cannot be held by empty gestures.' Mencius said: 'Our physical form and appearance are given by Heaven's nature. Only a sage can fully live up to the potential of this form.' King Xuan of Qi wished to shorten the mourning period. Gongsun Chou asked: 'Is not a mourning period of one year still better than none at all?' Mencius said: 'That is like someone twisting his elder brother's arm, and you telling him: "Just do it slowly and gently." You should simply teach him filial piety and brotherly respect.' A prince whose mother had died — his tutor requested a mourning period of several months on his behalf. Gongsun Chou asked: 'What about a case like this?' Mencius said: 'This is someone who wished to mourn the full period but could not obtain permission. Even adding a single day is better than nothing — this was said about those who could mourn but chose not to, when no one was preventing them.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「君子之所以教者五：有如時雨化之者，有成德者，有達財者，有答問者，有私淑艾者。此五者，君子之所以教也。」公孫丑曰：「道則高矣，美矣，宜若登天然，似不可及也。何不使彼為可幾及而日孳孳也？」孟子曰：「大匠不為拙工改廢繩墨，羿不為拙射變其彀率。君子引而不發，躍如也。中道而立，能者從之。」孟子曰：「天下有道，以道殉身；天下無道，以身殉道。未聞以道殉乎人者也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'The noble person teaches in five ways: There is the transforming influence that falls like timely rain. There is the perfecting of virtue. There is the developing of talent. There is the answering of questions. And there is the setting of an example that others study and emulate on their own. These five are the ways the noble person teaches.' Gongsun Chou said: 'The Way is lofty and beautiful indeed, but it seems like trying to climb to Heaven — apparently beyond reach. Why not make it something people can nearly attain, so they will strive for it day by day?' Mencius said: 'A master carpenter does not alter or abandon the plumb line for the sake of a clumsy worker. Yi the archer did not change his standard of pull for the sake of a clumsy archer. The noble person draws the bow fully but does not release the arrow — he only leaps forward as if about to shoot. He takes his stand in the middle of the path; those who are able will follow.' Mencius said: 'When the Way prevails in the world, the Way accompanies your person. When the Way does not prevail in the world, your person accompanies the Way. I have never heard of the Way being bent to accommodate another person.'

passages.text: 公都子曰：「滕更之在門也，若在所禮。而不答，何也？」孟子曰：「挾貴而問，挾賢而問，挾長而問，挾有勳勞而問，挾故而問，皆所不答也。滕更有二焉。」孟子曰：「於不可已而已者，無所不已；於所厚者薄，無所不薄也。其進銳者，其退速。」孟子曰：「君子之於物也，愛之而弗仁；於民也，仁之而弗親。親親而仁民，仁民而愛物。」
passages.translation_en: Gongdu Zi said: 'When Teng Geng was at your school, he seemed to be one who deserved courteous treatment. Yet you did not answer his questions — why?' Mencius said: 'Those who question while relying on their noble rank, or relying on their reputation for virtue, or relying on their seniority, or relying on their past services, or relying on old friendship — I do not answer any of these. Teng Geng had two of these faults.' Mencius said: 'If one stops where one should not stop, there is nothing at which one will not stop. If one is stingy where one should be generous, there is nothing toward which one will not be stingy. One who advances too eagerly will retreat just as quickly.' Mencius said: 'The noble person's attitude toward things is to care for them but not with benevolence. His attitude toward the people is to be benevolent but not with the love reserved for family. He loves his family and extends benevolence to the people; he is benevolent to the people and extends care to all things.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「知者無不知也，當務之為急；仁者無不愛也，急親賢之為務。堯舜之知而不遍物，急先務也；堯舜之仁不遍愛人，急親賢也。不能三年之喪，而緦小功之察；放飯流歠，而問無齒決，是之謂不知務。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'The wise person understands everything, but treats what is most pressing as urgent. The benevolent person loves everyone, but treats the befriending of the worthy as the priority. Even Yao and Shun's wisdom could not extend to everything — they focused on what was most urgent. Even Yao and Shun's benevolence could not extend love to every person — they focused on befriending the worthy. If one cannot observe the three-year mourning period yet is meticulous about the minor mourning rites of five months and three months; if one gobbles food and guzzles drink yet fusses over whether dried meat should be bitten through with the teeth — this is what is called not understanding priorities.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「不仁哉，梁惠王也！仁者以其所愛及其所不愛，不仁者以其所不愛及其所愛。」公孫丑問曰：「何謂也？」「梁惠王以土地之故，糜爛其民而戰之，大敗，將復之，恐不能勝，故驅其所愛子弟以殉之，是之謂以其所不愛及其所愛也。」孟子曰：「《春秋》無義戰。彼善於此，則有之矣。征者上伐下也，敵國不相征也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'How lacking in benevolence King Hui of Liang was! The benevolent extend their love from those they love to those they do not love. The unbenevolent extend their neglect from those they do not love to those they love.' Gongsun Chou asked: 'What do you mean?' 'King Hui of Liang, for the sake of territory, ground up his people in battle and suffered a great defeat. When he wanted to try again but feared he could not win, he drove his beloved sons and younger brothers to their deaths as well. This is what is meant by extending neglect from those one does not love to those one loves.' Mencius said: 'In the Spring and Autumn Annerta there are no righteous wars. Some were better than others, to be sure. "Punitive expeditions" are waged by superiors against inferiors — states of equal rank do not launch punitive expeditions against each other.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「盡信《書》，則不如無《書》。吾於《武成》，取二三策而已矣。仁人無敵於天下。以至仁伐至不仁，而何其血之流杵也？」孟子曰：「有人曰：『我善為陳，我善為戰。』大罪也。國君好仁，天下無敵焉。南面而征北狄怨，東面而征西夷怨。曰：『奚為後我？』武王之伐殷也，革車三百兩，虎賁三千人。王曰：『無畏！寧爾也，非敵百姓也。』若崩厥角稽首。征之為言正也，各欲正己也，焉用戰？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'If one believed everything in the Book of Documents, it would be better to have no Book of Documents at all. From the "Completion of the War" chapter, I accept only two or three strips. A benevolent man has no enemies in the world. When the supremely benevolent attacked the supremely unbenevolent, how could the blood have flowed until it floated the pestles?' Mencius said: 'If someone says, "I am expert at formations, I am expert at warfare," that is a great crime. If a ruler loves benevolence, he will have no enemies in the world. When King Wu marched south to punish, the northern tribes complained; when he marched east, the western tribes complained, saying, "Why does he leave us for last?" When King Wu attacked the Yin, he had three hundred war chariots and three thousand brave warriors. He proclaimed: "Do not fear! I come to bring you peace, not to fight the people." They bowed down, pressing their foreheads to the ground like a wall collapsing. To "punish" means to "correct" — when each wishes to be corrected, what need is there for war?'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「梓匠輪輿能與人規矩，不能使人巧。」孟子曰：「舜之飯糗茹草也，若將終身焉；及其為天子也，被袗衣，鼓琴，二女果，若固有之。」孟子曰：「吾今而後知殺人親之重也：殺人之父，人亦殺其父；殺人之兄，人亦殺其兄。然則非自殺之也，一閒耳。」孟子曰：「古之為關也，將以禦暴。今之為關也，將以為暴。」孟子曰：「身不行道，不行於妻子；使人不以道，不能行於妻子。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'A carpenter or wheelwright can give someone the compass and square, but cannot make them skilled.' Mencius said: 'When Shun was eating coarse rice and wild greens, it seemed as if he would live that way forever. Yet when he became Son of Heaven, wearing fine robes, playing the lute, with the two daughters of Yao attending him, it was as if he had always had these things.' Mencius said: 'Now I understand how grave it is to kill a man's kin. Kill a man's father, and he will kill your father; kill a man's brother, and he will kill your brother. You did not kill them with your own hands, but you are only one step removed.' Mencius said: 'The border passes of ancient times were meant to guard against violence. The border passes of today are meant to inflict violence.' Mencius said: 'If you do not practice the Way yourself, it will not be followed even by your wife and children. If you direct others without the Way, you cannot govern even your wife and children.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「周于利者，凶年不能殺；周于德者，邪世不能亂。」孟子曰：「好名之人，能讓千乘之國；苟非其人，簞食豆羹見於色。」孟子曰：「不信仁賢，則國空虛。無禮義，則上下亂。無政事，則財用不足。」孟子曰：「不仁而得國者，有之矣；不仁而得天下，未之有也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'One who is rich in principles cannot be destroyed by a bad year; one who is rich in virtue cannot be corrupted by a wicked age.' Mencius said: 'A man who loves fame can give away a state of a thousand chariots; but if he is not truly such a man, his displeasure shows over a bowl of rice and a cup of soup.' Mencius said: 'If the benevolent and worthy are not trusted, the state will be hollow and empty. Without ritual and righteousness, the relations between high and low will be in disorder. Without good governance, resources will be insufficient.' Mencius said: 'There have been cases of the unbenevolent gaining a state, but never has the unbenevolent gained the whole world.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「民為貴，社稷次之，君為輕。是故得乎丘民而為天子，得乎天子為諸侯，得乎諸侯為大夫。諸侯危社稷，則變置。犧牲既成，粢盛既潔，祭祀以時，然而旱乾水溢，則變置社稷。」孟子曰：「聖人，百世之師也，伯夷、柳下惠是也。故聞伯夷之風者，頑夫廉，懦夫有立志；聞柳下惠之風者，薄夫敦，鄙夫寬。奮乎百世之上。百世之下，聞者莫不興起也。非聖人而能若是乎，而況於親炙之者乎？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'The people are the most important, the altars of soil and grain come next, and the ruler is the least important. Therefore, he who wins the hearts of the common people becomes Son of Heaven; he who wins the favor of the Son of Heaven becomes a feudal lord; he who wins the favor of a feudal lord becomes a minister. When a feudal lord endangers the altars of soil and grain, he is replaced. When the sacrificial animals are properly prepared, the grain offerings are clean, and sacrifices are performed at the proper times, yet there is still drought and flood, then the altars of soil and grain are replaced.' Mencius said: 'Sages are teachers for a hundred generations — Bo Yi and Liuxia Hui are such men. Thus, when those who hear of Bo Yi's example are stirred, the corrupt become scrupulous and the weak become resolute. When those who hear of Liuxia Hui's example are stirred, the mean become generous and the petty become tolerant. They inspired people a hundred generations ago, and a hundred generations later, all who hear of them are roused. Could any but sages have such effect? How much more so for those who knew them personally!'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「仁也者，人也。合而言之，道也。」孟子曰：「孔子之去魯，曰：『遲遲吾行也。』去父母國之道也。去齊，接淅而行，去他國之道也。」孟子曰：「君子之戹於陳蔡之閒，無上下之交也。」貉稽曰：「稽大不理於口。」孟子曰：「無傷也。士憎茲多口。《詩》云：『憂心悄悄，慍于群小。』孔子也。『肆不殄厥慍，亦不隕厥問。』文王也。」孟子曰：「賢者以其昭昭，使人昭昭；今以其昬昬，使人昭昭。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'Benevolence is what it means to be human. To speak of them together — that is the Way.' Mencius said: 'When Confucius left Lu, he said, "I will go slowly, slowly." That is how one leaves the land of one's parents. When he left Qi, he drained his rice from the washing water and set off at once. That is how one leaves another state.' Mencius said: 'The reason the gentleman was besieged between Chen and Cai was that he had no connections with those in high or low positions.' Mo Ji said: 'I am much maligned by gossip.' Mencius said: 'That does no harm. Scholars are always subject to much gossip. The Odes say: "My heart is sad and troubled, I am resented by the petty crowd" — that was Confucius. And: "Though he could not stop their resentment, he did not let his reputation fall" — that was King Wen.' Mencius said: 'The worthy of old used their own clarity to bring clarity to others. People today try to use their own confusion to bring clarity to others.'

passages.text: 孟子謂高子曰：「山徑之蹊閒，介然用之而成路。為閒不用，則茅塞之矣。今茅塞子之心矣。」高子曰：「禹之聲，尚文王之聲。」孟子曰：「何以言之？」曰：「以追蠡。」曰：「是奚足哉？城門之軌，兩馬之力與？」齊饑。陳臻曰：「國人皆以夫子將復為發棠，殆不可復。」孟子曰：「是為馮婦也。晉人有馮婦者，善搏虎，卒為善士。則之野，有眾逐虎。虎負嵎，莫之敢攖。望見馮婦，趨而迎之。馮婦攘臂下車。眾皆悅之，其為士者笑之。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said to Gaozi: 'A trail through the mountains — if used constantly, it becomes a road. If unused for a time, it is choked with weeds. Now weeds have choked your mind.' Gaozi said: 'The music of Yu was superior to that of King Wen.' Mencius said: 'What makes you say so?' 'The hub of Yu's bell is more worn.' 'Is that sufficient evidence? The ruts at a city gate — were they carved by only two horses?' There was a famine in Qi. Chen Zhen said: 'The people all think you will again open the granary at Tang, as before. I fear it cannot be done again.' Mencius said: 'To do so would be acting like Feng Fu. In Jin there was a man named Feng Fu, famous for fighting tigers bare-handed. Eventually he became a reformed gentleman. Once, going to the countryside, he found a crowd chasing a tiger. The tiger had its back to a cliff and no one dared approach it. When they saw Feng Fu, they rushed to welcome him. Feng Fu rolled up his sleeves and stepped down from his carriage. The crowd was delighted — but the gentlemen among them laughed at him.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「口之於味也，目之於色也，耳之於聲也，鼻之於臭也，四肢之於安佚也，性也，有命焉，君子不謂性也。仁之於父子也，義之於君臣也，禮之於賓主也，智之於賢者也，聖人之於天道也，命也，有性焉，君子不謂命也。」浩生不害問曰：「樂正子，何人也？」孟子曰：「善人也，信人也。」「何謂善？何謂信？」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'The mouth's relation to flavors, the eye's to colors, the ear's to sounds, the nose's to smells, the four limbs' desire for comfort — these are matters of nature, but there is also fate in them, so the gentleman does not call them simply nature. The claims of benevolence between parent and child, of righteousness between ruler and minister, of ritual between guest and host, of wisdom in the worthy, of the sage toward the Way of Heaven — these are matters of fate, but there is also nature in them, so the gentleman does not call them simply fate.' Haosheng Buhai asked: 'What sort of man is Yue Zhengzi?' Mencius said: 'A good man, a sincere man.' 'What do you mean by good? What do you mean by sincere?'

passages.text: 曰：「可欲之謂善，有諸己之謂信。充實之謂美，充實而有光輝之謂大，大而化之之謂聖，聖而不可知之之謂神。樂正子，二之中，四之下也。」孟子曰：「逃墨必歸於楊，逃楊必歸於儒。歸，斯受之而已矣。今之與楊墨辯者，如追放豚，既入其苙，又從而招之。」孟子曰：「有布縷之征，粟米之征，力役之征。君子用其一，緩其二。用其二而民有殍，用其三而父子離。」孟子曰：「諸侯之寶三：土地，人民，政事。寶珠玉者，殃必及身。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'That which is desirable is called good. To have it within oneself is called sincere. To be filled with it is called beautiful. To be filled with it and radiant is called great. To be great and transform others is called sagely. To be sagely and beyond comprehension is called divine. Yue Zhengzi has attained the middle two of the first pair and falls below the last four.' Mencius said: 'Those who flee Mohism inevitably turn to Yangism; those who flee Yangism inevitably turn to Confucianism. When they return, simply accept them. Those who argue with Yangists and Mohists today are like chasing stray pigs — after getting them back in the pen, they still go and tie their legs.' Mencius said: 'There are taxes in cloth, taxes in grain, and taxes in labor service. A gentleman uses one and eases the other two. If he uses two, the people starve; if he uses all three, fathers and sons are torn apart.' Mencius said: 'A feudal lord has three treasures: territory, people, and governance. One who treasures pearls and jade will surely bring disaster upon himself.'

passages.text: 盆成括仕於齊。孟子曰：「死矣盆成括！」盆成括見殺。門人問曰：「夫子何以知其將見殺？」曰：「其為人也小有才，未聞君子之大道也，則足以殺其軀而已矣。」孟子之滕，館於上宮。有業屨於牖上，館人求之弗得。或問之曰：「若是乎從者之廀也？」曰：「子以是為竊屨來與？」曰：「殆非也。夫子之設科也，往者不追，來者不距。苟以是心至，斯受之而已矣。」
passages.translation_en: Pen Cheng Kuo took office in Qi. Mencius said: 'Pen Cheng Kuo is a dead man!' When Pen Cheng Kuo was indeed killed, his disciples asked: 'Master, how did you know he would be killed?' He replied: 'He was a man of small talent who had never learned the great Way of the gentleman — that was just enough to get himself killed.' When Mencius went to Teng, he lodged in the Upper Palace. A pair of unfinished sandals was left on the windowsill, and the lodge keeper searched for them but could not find them. Someone asked: 'Is this how your followers pilfer things?' Mencius said: 'Do you think they came here to steal sandals?' The man said: 'Presumably not. But, Master, you set up your school so that those who depart are not pursued and those who come are not turned away. If they come with the right intention, you simply accept them.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「人皆有所不忍，達之於其所忍，仁也；人皆有所不為，達之於其所為，義也。人能充無欲害人之心，而仁不可勝用也；人能充無穿踰之心，而義不可勝用也。人能充無受爾汝之實，無所往而不為義也。士未可以言而言，是以言餂之也；可以言而不言，是以不言餂之也，是皆穿踰之類也。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'Everyone has things they cannot bear to do. To extend this to what they can bear — that is benevolence. Everyone has things they will not do. To extend this to what they will do — that is righteousness. If people can fully develop their feeling of not wanting to harm others, their benevolence will be inexhaustible. If people can fully develop their feeling against trespassing and theft, their righteousness will be inexhaustible. If people can fully develop their refusal to be addressed contemptuously, they will act rightly wherever they go. When a scholar speaks when it is not yet appropriate to speak, he is using words to curry favor. When he does not speak when it is appropriate to speak, he is using silence to curry favor. Both are of the same kind as trespassing and theft.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「言近而指遠者，善言也；守約而施博者，善道也。君子之言也，不下帶而道存焉。君子之守，修其身而天下平。人病舍其田而芸人之田，所求於人者重，而所以自任者輕。」孟子曰：「堯舜，性者也；湯武，反之也。動容周旋中禮者，盛德之至也；哭死而哀，非為生者也；經德不回，非以干祿也；言語必信，非以正行也。君子行法，以俟命而已矣。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'Words that are simple yet point to something far-reaching — those are good words. Principles that are concise yet broadly applicable — that is a good way. The gentleman's words stay close to everyday matters, yet the Way is present in them. The gentleman's cultivation begins with his own person, and from that the whole world finds peace. People err in neglecting their own fields to weed another's — demanding much of others while taking little responsibility themselves.' Mencius said: 'Yao and Shun possessed goodness by nature; Tang and Wu returned to it through effort. When every movement and gesture accords with ritual, that is the height of flourishing virtue. Weeping for the dead out of genuine grief, not to impress the living; practicing moral constancy without wavering, not to seek a salary; keeping one's word in speech, not to justify one's conduct — the gentleman follows the Way and awaits what fate brings.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「說大人，則藐之，勿視其巍巍然。堂高數仞，榱題數尺，我得志弗為也；食前方丈，侍妾數百人，我得志弗為也；般樂飲酒，驅騁田獵，後車千乘，我得志弗為也。在彼者，皆我所不為也；在我者，皆古之制也，吾何畏彼哉？」孟子曰：「養心莫善於寡欲。其為人也寡欲，雖有不存焉者，寡矣；其為人也多欲，雖有存焉者，寡矣。」曾皙嗜羊棗，而曾子不忍食羊棗。公孫丑問曰：「膾炙與羊棗孰美？」孟子曰：「膾炙哉！」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'When speaking to a great man, look down on him and pay no regard to his lofty airs. His hall may be several fathoms high, his rafters several feet wide — were I to achieve my aims, I would not have these. A feast spread ten feet before him, attended by hundreds of concubines — were I to achieve my aims, I would not have these. Drinking and reveling, galloping and hunting, with a thousand chariots in his train — were I to achieve my aims, I would not have these. All that he has is what I would not do; all that I have follows the ways of the ancients. Why should I stand in awe of him?' Mencius said: 'The best way to cultivate the mind is to have few desires. If a person has few desires, though some part of his good nature may be lost, it will be little. If a person has many desires, though some part of his good nature may be preserved, it will be little.' Zengxi was fond of sheep-dates, and so Zengzi could not bear to eat sheep-dates. Gongsun Chou asked: 'Which is better — minced meat and roast, or sheep-dates?' Mencius said: 'Minced meat and roast, of course!'

passages.text: 公孫丑曰：「然則曾子何為食膾炙而不食羊棗？」曰：「膾炙所同也，羊棗所獨也。諱名不諱姓，姓所同也，名所獨也。」萬章問曰：「孔子在陳曰：『盍歸乎來！吾黨之士狂簡，進取，不忘其初。』孔子在陳，何思魯之狂士？」孟子曰：「孔子『不得中道而與之，必也狂獧乎！狂者進取，獧者有所不為也』。孔子豈不欲中道哉？不可必得，故思其次也。」「敢問何如斯可謂狂矣？」曰：「如琴張、曾皙、牧皮者，孔子之所謂狂矣。」
passages.translation_en: Gongsun Chou said: 'Then why did Zengzi eat minced meat and roast but not sheep-dates?' Mencius replied: 'Minced meat and roast are what everyone likes; sheep-dates were what his father alone loved. One avoids the personal name but not the surname — the surname is shared, the personal name is unique.' Wan Zhang asked: 'When Confucius was in Chen, he said, "Why not go home! The young scholars of my school are ambitious and eager, rushing forward to seize their goals, never forgetting their original ideals." Since Confucius was in Chen, why did he think longingly of the impetuous scholars of Lu?' Mencius said: 'Confucius said, "If I cannot find those who follow the middle way to associate with, I must turn to the impetuous and the cautious. The impetuous press forward; the cautious refrain from certain things." Would Confucius not have preferred those of the middle way? He could not be sure of finding them, so he thought of the next best.' 'May I ask what makes someone impetuous?' 'Men like Qin Zhang, Zengxi, and Mu Pi — these are those whom Confucius called impetuous.'

passages.text: 「何以謂之狂也？」曰：「其志嘐嘐然，曰『古之人，古之人』。夷考其行而不掩焉者也。狂者又不可得，欲得不屑不潔之士而與之，是獧也，是又其次也。孔子曰：『過我門而不入我室，我不憾焉者，其惟鄉原乎！鄉原，德之賊也。』」曰：「何如斯可謂之鄉原矣？」曰：「『何以是嘐嘐也？言不顧行，行不顧言，則曰：古之人，古之人。行何為踽踽涼涼？生斯世也，為斯世也，善斯可矣。』閹然媚於世也者，是鄉原也。」
passages.translation_en: 'Why were they called impetuous?' 'Their ambitions were lofty, always saying, "The ancients! The ancients!" But when you examine their conduct, it does not measure up to their words. If the impetuous too cannot be found, then one wishes for those who disdain to do what is unclean — these are the cautious, and they are yet another step below. Confucius said: "Those who pass my door without entering my house — the only ones I do not regret missing are the village worthies. The village worthy is the thief of virtue."' 'What makes someone a village worthy?' 'Those who say: "Why be so lofty in your ambitions? Their words take no account of their deeds, their deeds take no account of their words. Why go on about the ancients, the ancients? Why walk about so cold and aloof? Born in this age, be of this age — just being thought good is enough." Those who ingratiatingly court the favor of the world — these are the village worthies.'

passages.text: 萬子曰：「一鄉皆稱原人焉，無所往而不為原人，孔子以為德之賊，何哉？」曰：「非之無舉也，刺之無刺也；同乎流俗，合乎汙世；居之似忠信，行之似廉潔；眾皆悅之，自以為是，而不可與入堯舜之道，故曰德之賊也。孔子曰：『惡似而非者：惡莠，恐其亂苗也；惡佞，恐其亂義也；惡利口，恐其亂信也；惡鄭聲，恐其亂樂也；惡紫，恐其亂朱也；惡鄉原，恐其亂德也。』君子反經而已矣。經正，則庶民興；庶民興，斯無邪慝矣。」
passages.translation_en: Wan Zhang said: 'If everyone in a village praises someone as a worthy person, and he is a worthy person wherever he goes, why did Confucius call him a thief of virtue?' Mencius replied: 'Try to condemn him — there is nothing to point to. Try to criticize him — there is nothing to criticize. He goes along with the vulgar current and accords with the corrupt age. In his daily life he appears loyal and trustworthy; in his conduct he appears upright and clean. Everyone is pleased with him, and he considers himself right. Yet he cannot enter the Way of Yao and Shun — that is why he is called a thief of virtue. Confucius said: "I hate what resembles but is not genuine. I hate weeds, for fear they be confused with the grain. I hate flattery, for fear it be confused with righteousness. I hate a clever tongue, for fear it be confused with sincerity. I hate the music of Zheng, for fear it corrupt proper music. I hate purple, for fear it be confused with vermilion. I hate the village worthy, for fear he corrupt virtue." The gentleman simply returns to the standard. When the standard is correct, the common people will be stirred to goodness. When the common people are stirred, there will be no more wickedness.'

passages.text: 孟子曰：「由堯舜至於湯，五百有餘歲，若禹、皋陶，則見而知之；若湯，則聞而知之。由湯至於文王，五百有餘歲，若伊尹、萊朱則見而知之；若文王，則聞而知之。由文王至於孔子，五百有餘歲，若太公望、散宜生，則見而知之；若孔子，則聞而知之。由孔子而來至於今，百有餘歲，去聖人之世，若此其未遠也；近聖人之居，若此其甚也，然而無有乎爾，則亦無有乎爾。」
passages.translation_en: Mencius said: 'From Yao and Shun to Tang was over five hundred years. Men like Yu and Gao Yao knew the Way by seeing it firsthand; Tang knew it by hearing of it. From Tang to King Wen was over five hundred years. Men like Yi Yin and Lai Zhu knew the Way by seeing it firsthand; King Wen knew it by hearing of it. From King Wen to Confucius was over five hundred years. Men like Taigong Wang and San Yisheng knew the Way by seeing it firsthand; Confucius knew it by hearing of it. From Confucius to the present is over a hundred years. The distance from the sage's time is so short; the proximity to the sage's home is so close. Yet if there is no one to carry it on — then indeed there will be no one to carry it on.'
